title: What Would We Predict Before Fitting Anything?
blurb: Tomorrow's water demand is unknown. Yesterday's demand gives Botie a prediction he can actually make, and a reference that a more complicated forecast should improve on.
openingTitle: How Much Water Should Botie Prepare for Tomorrow?
opening: Botie records how many litres the greenhouse uses each day. He needs to prepare tomorrow's supply before tomorrow's measurement exists. The order of these observations now matters: a good explanation of yesterday is not necessarily a useful prediction made the day before.

Let's begin with a rule that requires no fitted coefficients. Predict the most recently observed demand. We can make that prediction, wait for the next day, and record the difference. That small procedure gives every later model a fair starting comparison.

history.title: Giving a Forecast a Reference to Beat

sources.title: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos: The Forecaster's Toolbox

blocks: Forecasting grew around decisions that had to be made before demand, production, or other measurements were known. A method needed to earn its complexity against forecasts available from the existing record. Hyndman and Athanasopoulos's forecasting text formalises simple rules as benchmarks in this workflow.

We will begin by predicting that tomorrow's demand equals the latest observed demand. This is a naive, or persistence, forecast. Our greenhouse record is invented so we can check every prediction. A more complicated method should be compared with this rule on the same future days.

intuition.title: Stop at the prediction time
intuition.explanation: Only three daily totals have arrived. Tomorrow's value must remain outside the input.

intuition.title: Write a prediction before looking
intuition.explanation: The persistence rule copies the latest available total.

intuition.title: Reveal the next observation
intuition.explanation: Suppose the next day uses 14 litres. Keep the earlier prediction rather than rewriting it after seeing this result.

parts.title: 1. Separate the Forecast Origin From Its Target
paragraphs: The forecast origin is when we make a prediction. The horizon is how far ahead its target lies. A daily one-step forecast predicts the next day's value using information available now.
Keep timestamps, measurement units, and sampling intervals with the series. Missing days are not automatically zero-demand days, and a list of irregular readings is not automatically a daily series.
parts.calculation:
Origin: end of Tuesday
Horizon: one day
Target: Wednesday's total demand
interpretation: The information boundary matters more than whether a rule is simple or learned.

parts.title: 2. Try Persistence and a Historical Mean
paragraphs: Persistence copies the latest observation. A historical-mean forecast averages a chosen training history. The first follows recent level changes quickly; the second smooths fluctuations but can lag behind a real change.
Choose the history before seeing the target. For a multiple-day forecast made at one origin, persistence repeats the same last known value for every horizon; it cannot copy future observations.
parts.calculation:
Known values = [10,12,11]
Persistence forecast = 11
Historical-mean forecast = (10 + 12 + 11) / 3 = 11
interpretation: Agreement on this short record does not make the rules equivalent.

parts.title: 3. Score Predictions That Were Made in Time
paragraphs: Compare each recorded prediction with its later observation. Absolute error keeps the size of a mistake in the original units. Average it over the same target days for every competing method.
Do not confuse fitted residuals with genuine forecast errors. A model fitted using the target's own date has received information unavailable at the earlier origin.
parts.calculation:
Observations = [10,12,11,14]
One-step persistence predictions = [10,12,11]
Targets = [12,11,14]
MAE = (2 + 1 + 3) / 3 = 2
interpretation: The first observation has no preceding value here, so it is not scored.

examples.title: One forecast, recorded before the next reading
paragraphs: Suppose the last three daily totals are known. We copy the most recent one before revealing the next day's water use, then measure the size of the miss.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
history = np.array([10., 12., 11.])
forecast = history[-1]
observed_next_day = 14.0
print(float(forecast))
print(float(abs(observed_next_day - forecast)))
interpretation: The forecast stays at eleven litres when the fourteen-litre observation arrives. The later value belongs in the error calculation, not in the earlier prediction.

parts.title: 4. Keep the Baseline While the Model Changes
paragraphs: Weather, opening hours, and planting schedules might improve the prediction. We will add those kinds of structure gradually, retaining a baseline on the same held-out dates.

A forecast is not a stock decision by itself. Preparing too little water may have a different cost from preparing too much. This lesson establishes point predictions; later evaluation can account for those consequences.
interpretation: Botie's construction compares the preceding-day predictions and target days supplied separately.

parts.title: 5. Yesterday May Be the Wrong Day to Copy
paragraphs: If greenhouse demand follows a watering schedule, the most recent day in the same schedule position can be a stronger baseline than yesterday. A seasonal-naive forecast repeats that earlier observation.

The seasonal period must describe the actual calendar or process. Seven array positions mean one week only when the record really contains one position per day. Missing days need explicit treatment before we use a positional lag.

parts.title: 6. Forecast a Whole Schedule from One Origin
paragraphs: At a single forecast origin, none of the future observations are available. A multi-step seasonal baseline repeats values from the most recent observed cycle, wrapping around that cycle when necessary.
Keep those forecasts together as one issued forecast. Updating them after tomorrow's reading arrives creates a forecast from a later origin, which should be scored separately.

examples.title: Repeat a three-day irrigation cycle
paragraphs: The most recent complete cycle used 10, 14 and 8 litres. Botie needs five future daily forecasts now.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
last_cycle = np.array([10.,14.,8.])
horizon = 5
forecast = last_cycle[np.arange(horizon) % len(last_cycle)]
print(forecast.tolist())
interpretation: The cycle repeats because that is the baseline assumption. A changed watering schedule is a direct reason for the rule to fail.

parts.title: 7. Keep a Separate Error for Each Horizon
paragraphs: A method that is useful tomorrow may be poor a week ahead. Retain origin, target date, horizon, forecast and eventual observation for every prediction. Compare methods only where those keys match.

Inspect peak-demand days and under-prediction as well as overall absolute error. If running out of water is much more costly than carrying excess, the decision may require a quantile or a stock policy rather than a mean forecast alone.

title: Building Inputs From Earlier Days
blurb: A prediction row needs information available before its target. We will turn one ordered record into rows of earlier readings without accidentally including the answer.
openingTitle: Which Readings Could Botie Have Used That Morning?
opening: A regression model expects rows of inputs and corresponding answers. Botie's demand log is just one sequence. We need to decide which earlier entries belong beside each future target before we can fit anything.
For each target day, take the two preceding days in chronological order. Then slide that window forward by one position. Keeping the dates aligned is the first part of building a forecasting model.

history.title: Turning Delayed Effects Into Predictors
blocks: Many processes respond after a delay: an earlier input can influence a later outcome. Dynamic regression includes lagged predictors to represent that timing. The important modelling choice is which past information was available and which delay it could plausibly have.
Our first example uses earlier demand to predict later demand. This constructs a supervised table from a time record; it does not establish that an earlier reading causes the next one.

intuition.title: Keep a target aside
intuition.explanation: The third value is the first target with two preceding observations.

intuition.title: Move the window one position
intuition.explanation: The former target becomes a known input only after its observation time.

intuition.title: Keep column meanings fixed
intuition.explanation: The first column is older and the second is more recent in every row.

parts.title: 1. Define What One Row Represents
paragraphs: Each row will represent one forecast: the readings available when we make it, paired with the later value we want to predict. With two lags here, the older reading goes in column zero and the newer one in column one. We must use that order when predicting too.

The first two dates do not have enough preceding readings for complete rows. We omit them. Filling that unavailable history with zeros would tell the model that measurements existed when they did not.
interpretation: The target is the entry immediately after each input window.

parts.title: 2. Use a Trailing Summary When Individual Lags Are Unnecessary
paragraphs: A trailing mean summarises only the past window. It can reduce sensitivity to a single noisy reading, at the cost of discarding the order within that window.

A centred moving average is different: it can include observations after the position being summarised. That can help retrospective smoothing but can leak future information if used carelessly as a forecasting feature.
parts.calculation:
First trailing mean = (4 + 6) / 2 = 5
Second trailing mean = (6 + 5) / 2 = 5.5
interpretation: We calculate each summary from its input row before examining the target.

parts.title: 3. Keep Real Availability Separate From the Timestamp
paragraphs: A weather forecast issued yesterday might be available now, while tomorrow's measured rainfall is not. A record's measurement date alone does not prove it was available when a prediction was made.

Historical backtests should reproduce publication delays, late corrections, and missing readings where they matter. Replacing an old forecast with today's revised record can create an unrealistically easy problem.
interpretation: Lagging a column is necessary in some tasks, but it is not a complete availability audit.

examples.title: Build the row for one target day
paragraphs: The first prediction with two lags needs two earlier readings. Separate those inputs from the next value before building a whole table.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
readings = np.array([10, 12, 11, 15])
target_position = 2
features = readings[target_position - 2:target_position]
target = readings[target_position]
print(features.tolist())
print(int(target))
interpretation: The feature slice stops before the target position. Practice will repeat this alignment across every eligible target date.

parts.title: 4. Construct and Inspect Before Fitting
paragraphs: Print a few input rows with their target dates. Check the first and last rows manually, including the oldest and newest entries. This often reveals an off-by-one error more clearly than a model score does.
Botie's workshop constructs the past-only rows and averages each row. It is a moving-mean predictor, not an autoregressive model with fitted coefficients.
interpretation: The next lessons decide what structure to model once the table is aligned.

parts.title: 5. Choose the Target Horizon before Building Rows
paragraphs: For a one-day forecast, the label follows the newest feature immediately. For a two-day forecast, an extra day lies between the newest available observation and the target. Shifting the feature window without shifting the target accordingly changes the task.
Print the first and last training rows with their time positions before fitting. This catches off-by-one errors more clearly than inspecting a final model score.

examples.title: Build two-day targets from two known lags
paragraphs: The forecast origin is the index of the newest known reading. The target is two positions later.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([10.,12.,14.,16.,18.,20.])
rows, targets = [], []
for origin in range(1, len(y)-2):
    rows.append(y[origin-1:origin+1])
    targets.append(y[origin+2])
print(np.array(rows).tolist())
print([float(value) for value in targets])
interpretation: The intervening reading is not a feature. It would be unavailable at the stated origin.

parts.title: 6. A Future Calendar Entry and a Future Temperature Are Different Inputs
paragraphs: Tomorrow's weekday or a scheduled watering event may already be known today. Tomorrow's actual temperature is not. A forecast can use a weather forecast issued today, but training must use comparable historical forecasts rather than the later observed weather.
Record issue times for external inputs. Revised forecasts and backfilled measurements can leak later information into a retrospective feature table even when the target column is shifted correctly.

task: Write lag_table(y, lags, horizon). y is a finite one-dimensional numerical series; lags and horizon are positive integers. Each row contains lags consecutive observations from oldest to newest. Its target lies horizon positions after the newest input.

Return the two-dimensional input table and one-dimensional targets. Require enough observations for at least one row, preserve y and raise ValueError for invalid input. Print the demonstration arrays as lists.

def lag_table(y, lags, horizon):
    # Write the procedure here.

practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def lag_table(y, lags, horizon):
    y = np.asarray(y, dtype=float)
    if y.ndim != 1 or not np.isfinite(y).all() or any(isinstance(v,bool) or not isinstance(v,(int,np.integer)) or v < 1 for v in [lags,horizon]):
        raise ValueError('Invalid series or window')
    count = len(y)-lags-horizon+1
    if count < 1:
        raise ValueError('Insufficient history')
    X = np.array([y[start:start+lags] for start in range(count)])
    target = np.array([y[start+lags+horizon-1] for start in range(count)])
    return X, target

X, y = lag_table([3,5,8,12,17,23], 2, 2)
print(X.tolist())
print(y.tolist())
hints: The newest input is at start + lags - 1.
Add horizon to that position to locate its target.

title: Separating Repetition From Change
blurb: A demand increase might be a lasting change or a normal part of the weekly schedule. Comparing like positions in a cycle helps us distinguish those possibilities.
openingTitle: Is Demand Growing, or Is It Monday Again?
opening: Botie sees high demand every time a scheduled irrigation cycle begins. A model that treats each rise as a new upward trend will repeatedly overreact. We need to compare today's demand with a relevant earlier position.

An ordinary difference compares neighbouring observations. A seasonal difference compares observations one full cycle apart. Let's see which pattern each comparison removes and what information we must keep to return to the original units.

history.title: Describing Changes When Levels Would Not Sit Still
blocks: Time-series modelling developed tools for records whose levels or recurring patterns changed over time. Differencing became a central part of the Box-Jenkins ARIMA approach: model changes when a more stable relationship can be expressed there.

Let's try differencing on a record where we know the trend and repeating cycle we put into it. We can watch what each subtraction removes. A real record may retain changing behaviour afterwards, so differencing is something to inspect, not an automatic guarantee of stationarity.

intuition.title: A rising level
intuition.explanation: Adjacent observations increase by the same amount in this invented record.

intuition.title: Look at the changes
intuition.explanation: Neighbouring differences remove this particular linear trend.

intuition.title: Compare matching cycle positions
intuition.explanation: With a two-position cycle, compare each reading with the one two steps earlier.

parts.title: 1. Name Trend, Seasonality, and Irregular Variation
paragraphs: A trend is a persistent movement in level. Seasonality is a pattern recurring at a known calendar or sampling period. Irregular variation includes changes these descriptions do not explain.

Do not infer a reliable seasonal pattern from one repetition. Inspect several cycles and understand the schedule that might produce it. A changing sampling interval can also make an apparent period misleading.
parts.calculation:
Example period = 2 observations
Matching positions: 0 with 2, 1 with 3
interpretation: The period counts observations here, not an unspecified number of days.

parts.title: 2. Subtract a Relevant Earlier Level
paragraphs: An ordinary first difference removes the previous observation. A seasonal difference removes the observation one period earlier. The operations ask different questions and can sometimes be combined.

A stable-looking difference series is evidence to inspect, not proof that all distributional properties remain constant. Stationarity is stronger than simply having no obvious trend in one short plot.
parts.calculation:
Ordinary difference: d[t] = y[t] - y[t-1]
Seasonal difference: d[t] = y[t] - y[t-period]
interpretation: The transformation discards initial levels from its output. Keep them for inversion.

parts.title: 3. Return a Change Forecast to the Original Units
paragraphs: If a model predicts tomorrow's ordinary difference, add it to the last observed level to obtain tomorrow's level forecast. For later horizons, use earlier predicted levels when the actual future levels are still unavailable.
For seasonal differences, use the matching seasonal reference. Depending on the horizon, that reference may itself be a forecast. Record which quantities are measured and which are predicted.
parts.calculation:
Last observed level = 16
Predicted next change = 2
Next level forecast = 16 + 2 = 18
interpretation: A forecast in differenced units cannot be compared directly with an observed level.

examples.title: Compare two positions with their previous cycle
paragraphs: Here the illustrative pattern repeats every two readings. Put the earlier cycle beside the later one so each subtraction compares the same position.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
earlier_cycle = np.array([8, 12])
later_cycle = np.array([11, 13])
change = later_cycle - earlier_cycle
print(change.tolist())
print((earlier_cycle + change).tolist())
interpretation: The changes retain their cycle positions. Adding them to the correct earlier values recovers the later levels; differences alone do not preserve the original level.

parts.title: 4. Avoid Removing More Structure Than Necessary
paragraphs: Differencing a series that was already stable can amplify noise and create unnecessary dependence between adjacent changes. Decide the transformation from training history and diagnostics, then evaluate the complete forecasting procedure.
The workshop calculates seasonal changes with a supplied period. Try a period of one to recover ordinary differencing, and a repeating cycle to see zero seasonal changes.
interpretation: Seasonal naive forecasting instead copies the previous matching level directly. It provides a useful baseline without fitting a model to the differences.

parts.title: 5. A Difference Forecast Still Needs a Starting Level
paragraphs: Predicting a change removes the level from the model's target. To recover demand, add the predicted change to the last known level. At later horizons, keep adding changes to the level reconstructed so far.

Seasonal differences use a different reference: the corresponding earlier season position. If that reference lies in the forecast future, use the previously reconstructed forecast, not a secretly available observation. Save the initial history required to undo every transformation.

parts.title: 6. Rebuild Demand from Predicted Daily Changes
paragraphs: The first forecast begins from the last observed demand. Each later forecast begins from the preceding forecast. Cumulative sums express this recurrence once the changes have been predicted.
The example supplies changes to isolate the inversion. It does not fit a model or establish that these changes are predictable.

examples.title: Undo ordinary differencing
paragraphs: The last observed demand is 20 litres.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
last = 20.
predicted_change = np.array([2., -1., 3.])
level = last + np.cumsum(predicted_change)
print(level.tolist())
print(np.diff(np.r_[last, level]).tolist())
interpretation: Differencing the reconstructed path recovers the supplied changes, which checks the bookkeeping.

parts.title: 7. Differencing Also Changes the Noise
paragraphs: Subtracting adjacent noisy readings includes noise from both readings. Consecutive differences share one of those noise terms with opposite signs, so differencing can introduce negative short-lag dependence even when the original noise was independent.

Do not repeatedly difference until a plot merely looks flat. Compare suitable models and inspect residuals. A trend, a seasonal pattern, a level shift and a measurement fault can require different explanations despite all producing visible changes over time.

title: Updating a Forecast Without Starting Over
blurb: Botie needs to respond to new demand without letting one unusual day replace everything he knows. A weighted update lets him control how quickly his estimate changes.
openingTitle: How Much Should One New Day Change the Estimate?
opening: Yesterday's demand may be useful, but it can also be unusually high or low. Averaging the entire history has the opposite problem: old conditions may keep influencing the estimate after the greenhouse has changed.

We can retain a current estimate of demand and adjust it toward each new observation. The question becomes how much of the new discrepancy to use. That single choice produces a sequence of estimates we can inspect.

history.title: Maintaining a Level Estimate as Observations Arrive
blocks: Exponential smoothing emerged in forecasting work in the 1950s, including contributions associated with Brown and Holt. Forecasters needed practical updates for changing records, rather than repeatedly treating every old observation equally.

Simple exponential smoothing maintains a level. More elaborate versions add trend and seasonal states. We begin with the level-only update so its response to a new observation is visible before adding those components.

intuition.title: Keep the current estimate
intuition.explanation: Botie's current level is ten litres.

intuition.title: Observe a different day
intuition.explanation: The new reading is fourteen litres. With an update fraction of one quarter, only part of that discrepancy moves the level.

intuition.title: Carry the updated state forward
intuition.explanation: The updated level is eleven litres and becomes the next one-step forecast.

parts.title: 1. Separate Observation, State, and Forecast
paragraphs: Before today's reading arrives, Botie has yesterday's retained level estimate. He uses that to forecast today. Once the actual demand is known, he can update the level for tomorrow.
Keep those two moments separate in the code. If we update first and then score the result against today's reading, we are using part of the answer in what we call a forecast.
parts.calculation:
Before observation: forecast[t] = level[t-1]
After observation: update level[t]
interpretation: The order of operations prevents tomorrow's information from changing yesterday's saved prediction.

parts.title: 2. Move Partway Toward the New Reading
paragraphs: The smoothing parameter alpha lies between zero and one. A small value changes the estimate slowly; a large value responds quickly. Alpha zero ignores new data and alpha one replaces the level with the latest observation.
The error-correction form and weighted-average form describe the same update.
parts.calculation:
level_new = level_old + alpha × (reading - level_old)
= 10 + 0.25 × (14 - 10)
= 11
interpretation: The two weights in the equivalent average sum to one.

parts.title: 3. Understand Why Older Readings Fade
paragraphs: Repeated substitution shows that each older contribution is multiplied by another factor of one minus alpha at every update. Its influence decreases geometrically. The initial state also retains some influence until enough updates have occurred.
This explains the name exponential smoothing. It does not mean that the data itself is assumed to grow exponentially.
parts.calculation:
Weight on latest reading: alpha
Weight on preceding reading: alpha × (1-alpha)
Weight one step earlier: alpha × (1-alpha)^2
interpretation: Choose an initial state and record it when reproducing a calculation.

examples.title: Let one new day move the retained level
paragraphs: Botie predicted ten litres. The next day used fourteen, and we choose to absorb one quarter of that surprise into the level.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
level = 10.0
reading = 14.0
alpha = 0.25
forecast_before_reading = level
surprise = reading - level
level = level + alpha * surprise
print(f'{forecast_before_reading:.2f}')
print(f'{level:.2f}')
interpretation: The saved forecast is still ten. Eleven is the updated state for a later prediction. Keeping those two moments separate is the main job of the loop in practice.

parts.title: 4. Match the State to the Structure in the Series
paragraphs: Simple exponential smoothing gives a flat forecast beyond the current level. A persistent trend or seasonal pattern calls for additional structure or a different method.

Choose alpha using a training and validation procedure that respects time. Do not select it on final test outcomes. In the workshop, build one update and inspect how the old estimate and new reading each contribute.
interpretation: The Python loop repeats the same update over a record, saving predictions before each new reading.

parts.title: 5. Choose Alpha by Forecasting before Updating
paragraphs: A candidate alpha defines an entire sequence of states. For each candidate, reset to the same initial state, save a forecast, observe the target and only then update. Score all candidates on matching validation targets.
Updating before saving the prediction evaluates how well the smoother explains a value it has already seen. That produces an artificially favourable result, especially at a high alpha.

examples.title: Compare two response rates on an ordered record
paragraphs: Both candidates start from a level of ten. These supplied observations illustrate validation bookkeeping.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
observed = np.array([12.,14.,13.])
for alpha in [.2,.8]:
    level = 10.
    errors = []
    for value in observed:
        errors.append(abs(value-level))
        level += alpha*(value-level)
    print(alpha, round(float(np.mean(errors)), 3))
interpretation: The faster response wins on these three targets. Select a rate on a proper validation period and retain a later period for final assessment.

parts.title: 6. A Trend Needs Its Own State
paragraphs: A level-only smoother keeps one current estimate and predicts that level at every future horizon. A steadily rising process needs another quantity: the estimated change per interval. A trend model updates both level and trend, then extends the level using the trend.

The extra state adds flexibility and another estimation problem. A temporary jump can be mistaken for persistent growth. Compare with the level-only and seasonal baselines rather than assuming an extra state must improve forecasts.

title: Learning From a Series' Own Past
blurb: A trailing average gives every lag the same influence. An autoregressive model fits different coefficients for the earlier readings and then uses that same rule to predict ahead.
openingTitle: Does Yesterday Matter More Than the Day Before?
opening: Botie's moving mean treats the previous two days equally. But demand may respond more strongly to the most recent day, or alternate with a schedule. We can let labelled historical input-target pairs determine those contributions.
The machinery is familiar regression. What changes is the source of its features and the care needed when using a prediction as the input to another prediction.

history.title: Predicting a Record From Earlier Values of Itself

sources.title: Yule: On a Method of Investigating Periodicities in Disturbed Series (1927)

blocks: Yule's 1927 work investigated disturbed periodic series by relating a value to earlier values of the same process. That gives us a way to learn how earlier readings contribute, while leaving a remainder for variation the relationship does not explain. We will use that idea with Botie's demand history.

Later ARIMA methods combined autoregressive terms with other components, including differencing. Our exercise fits a small autoregression directly with least squares; it is not an automatic ARIMA-selection procedure.

intuition.title: Keep the familiar supervised table
intuition.explanation: Earlier demand values form features; the following observation is the target.

intuition.title: Give the lags separate coefficients
intuition.explanation: A fitted rule can weight the newer value more heavily instead of imposing equal weights.

intuition.title: Use a forecast when a future reading is unavailable
intuition.explanation: Beyond one step, a recursive forecast shifts the history and inserts its own prediction.

parts.title: 1. Build the Regression Without Changing the Time Order
paragraphs: Each row contains a fixed number of preceding observations and one later target. Add a column of ones to fit an intercept. Least squares then finds coefficients that minimise squared training residuals.
Neighbouring rows overlap in their histories. Randomly splitting them can give an unrealistic evaluation of forecasting into a later period.
parts.calculation: prediction = intercept + older_weight × older + newer_weight × newer
interpretation: The column order is part of the fitted model and must travel with it.

parts.title: 2. Fit With a Linear Solver
paragraphs: Use a least-squares solver rather than explicitly inverting a matrix. The solver can handle an overdetermined design and report rank information. Perfectly correlated lag columns can make individual coefficients poorly determined even when predictions look reasonable.
Choose the lag count using time-respecting validation. More lags add parameters and can overfit a short record.
parts.calculation:
design = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X)), X])
coefficients = np.linalg.lstsq(design, targets, rcond=None)[0]
interpretation: Check predictions and held-out behaviour rather than treating every fitted coefficient as a causal explanation.

parts.title: 3. Distinguish One-Step and Recursive Forecasting
paragraphs: For a one-step forecast, every lag in the current window is observed. For later horizons from the same origin, some lag values are not yet known. A recursive procedure substitutes its previous predictions.
An alternative fits separate direct models for different horizons. These are different forecasting procedures and should be evaluated under the horizon they will actually serve.
interpretation: The second calculation uses a prediction, not a secretly revealed observation.

examples.title: Use one lag with already fitted coefficients
paragraphs: Before fitting a rule, check what its coefficients mean. This supplied rule combines an intercept with half of the latest reading.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
coefficients = np.array([1.0, 0.5])
latest_reading = 8.0
row = np.array([1.0, latest_reading])
contributions = row * coefficients
print(contributions.tolist())
print(float(contributions.sum()))
interpretation: The constant column contributes the intercept; the other column contributes the lagged demand. Practice will estimate coefficients from a new sequence instead of receiving them.

parts.title: 4. Inspect Stability and Uncertainty
paragraphs: Repeated application can magnify errors when a fitted recurrence is unstable. Even a stable fitted rule leaves unexplained variation, so a point forecast should not be read as a guarantee.

Plot residuals in time order, compare with simple baselines, and test on later origins. Uncertainty intervals need assumptions about future disturbances and parameter uncertainty, beyond the deterministic workshop calculation.
interpretation: Botie's construction applies supplied lag coefficients. The Python task also fits a one-lag model from a small historical sequence.

parts.title: 5. A Smooth Record Can Make Lag Coefficients Hard to Separate
paragraphs: When yesterday and the day before are almost identical across the training record, their columns contain nearly the same information. Many pairs of coefficients can give similar predictions. Individual coefficient interpretations become fragile even when the fitted curve looks stable.

Inspect the design rank and sensitivity to the training period. Regularisation may stabilise estimation, but coefficients in an observational forecasting rule do not become causal effects merely because a penalty was added.

parts.title: 6. A Small Error Can Grow during Recursive Forecasting
paragraphs: For a one-lag rule, a difference in the current value is multiplied by the lag coefficient at each recursive step. A magnitude above one amplifies that difference. More complicated lag models need a corresponding recurrence analysis.
This does not mean every growing series is invalid. It means a model intended to describe stable fluctuations must be checked against the behaviour of its fitted recurrence.

examples.title: Propagate the same initial forecast discrepancy
paragraphs: No new observations or disturbances are added. Only the recurrence changes.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
for coefficient in [.8, 1.2]:
    discrepancy = 1.
    path = []
    for _ in range(4):
        discrepancy *= coefficient
        path.append(round(discrepancy, 4))
    print(path)
interpretation: The second recurrence magnifies the original discrepancy. Forecast intervals must also account for new disturbances and parameter uncertainty, which this trace deliberately omits.

parts.title: 7. Residuals Can Still Contain a Schedule the Model Missed
paragraphs: Place residuals in time order. Repeated positive residuals at the same schedule position suggest structure that the fitted features did not explain. Compare residuals with lagged residuals and with known operating conditions.
Use those patterns to form a new modelling hypothesis, then test it on later data. Selecting many lags after repeatedly inspecting the final test period turns that period into model-development data.

title: Testing a Forecast as Time Moves Forward
blurb: One convenient cutoff can hide a forecasting failure. We will replay several prediction dates, preserving what was known at each one, and compare methods on matching targets.
openingTitle: Would This Rule Have Helped Before We Knew the Answer?
opening: Botie's forecast looks convincing on a plot of the whole record. But the model was fitted after all those observations existed. We need to reconstruct the decisions he could have made at earlier dates.

Move a cutoff through the record. At each cutoff, fit or update using only the available past, save the requested forecast, and score it against the later target. This makes the evaluation follow the intended use.

history.title: Replaying Earlier Forecast Origins

sources.title: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos: The Forecaster's Toolbox
Tashman: Out-of-Sample Tests of Forecasting Accuracy (2000)

blocks: Forecasting researchers needed evaluations that respected the order in which observations became available. Tashman's 2000 review discussed out-of-sample testing choices, including rolling origins, rather than treating one fitted historical curve as evidence of future accuracy.

Let's replay the decision at several earlier dates. At each date we expose only the observations that would have been available then, fit the procedure, and record its forecast before checking the later result. The small arrays let us inspect these time boundaries directly.

intuition.title: Make the first split
intuition.explanation: Train or initialise using the first three observations and predict the next one.

intuition.title: Move the origin
intuition.explanation: After the target is observed, extend the available history and make the following prediction.

intuition.title: Score matching targets
intuition.explanation: The two methods must be compared on these same target dates.

parts.title: 1. Choose Origins and Horizons Before Scoring
paragraphs: An expanding window retains all earlier training observations. A sliding window keeps a fixed recent span. The first can estimate from more data; the second can respond to a changed process by discarding older conditions.
Specify the forecast horizon, minimum history, update frequency, and training window before comparing scores. Different choices represent different deployment tasks.
parts.calculation:
Origin 3: history positions [0,1,2], target position 3
Origin 4: history positions [0,1,2,3], target position 4
interpretation: Array indices here identify chronological positions, not shuffled rows.

parts.title: 2. Refit the Whole Procedure Within Each Origin
paragraphs: Any learned scaling, imputation, feature selection, or model coefficients must be learned using that origin's training data. Fitting preprocessing once on the complete sequence still leaks future information even if the model's rows are split correctly.
When labels or measurements arrive late, move the usable cutoff back accordingly. The replay should match actual availability rather than an idealised instant report.
interpretation: A backtest evaluates the complete prediction procedure, including how often it is allowed to update.

parts.title: 3. Compare Errors at Matching Dates and Horizons
paragraphs: Calculate an error for each saved forecast and its target. Report overall summaries and inspect errors across time. Overlapping forecasts and shared training histories can make those errors dependent.
If a method predicts several horizons, report performance by horizon as well as any chosen aggregate. A good next-day forecast need not be a good next-month forecast.
parts.calculation:
Targets = [9,8]
Persistence errors = [3,1]; MAE = 2
Trailing-two errors = [2.5,0.5]; MAE = 1.5
interpretation: This tiny comparison illustrates bookkeeping. It is far too small to establish reliable superiority.

examples.title: Score two rules at one prediction date
paragraphs: Only the three history values are available when the prediction is made. We save both rules' answers and reveal the target afterwards.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
history = np.array([4., 6., 8.])
predictions = np.array([history[-1], history[-2:].mean()])
target = 10.0
print(predictions.tolist())
print(np.abs(target - predictions).tolist())
interpretation: Persistence does better at this one origin. That does not settle the comparison across a whole period; the challenge repeats the process at several dates.

parts.title: 4. Keep a Final Period Outside Model Selection
paragraphs: Use rolling validation to select settings, then evaluate the chosen procedure on a final untouched period. Repeatedly adjusting a model after inspecting that period turns it into another validation set.
Botie's workshop compares aligned absolute errors. The coding task creates those predictions from the historical record itself, then a second task checks performance separately by horizon.
interpretation: A deployment project later adds monitoring because the process can change after even a careful backtest.

parts.title: 5. A Forecast Origin Is Not Always the Latest Row in an Export
paragraphs: If daily demand is finalised the following afternoon, tomorrow morning's forecast cannot use yesterday's final total yet. Replaying the task requires both event dates and reporting dates.

At each origin, build the available history from records that had arrived by that time. A later corrected reading can be useful for scoring, but should not replace the version actually available to the historical predictor.

parts.title: 6. Compare an Expanding History with a Recent Window
paragraphs: An expanding window retains all past observations. A fixed recent window forgets older regimes. Neither is universally preferable: the first reduces estimation noise under stability, while the second can respond faster to change.
Choose the window rule using validation origins. Compare predictions on the same targets, including dates after a plausible operating change.

examples.title: Two historical means after a level change
paragraphs: The record shifts from a low-demand period to a high-demand period. Targets begin at position three.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([5.,5.,5.,10.,10.,10.])
for origin in [3,4,5]:
    expanding = y[:origin].mean()
    recent = y[origin-2:origin].mean()
    print(origin, round(float(expanding), 2), round(float(recent), 2), float(y[origin]))
interpretation: Both methods miss the first unannounced change. The recent window then adapts faster because it discards older conditions.

parts.title: 7. Preserve the Paired Errors before Averaging
paragraphs: Keep each method's error beside the same origin and horizon. The difference between their errors tells us on which decisions one helped. An overall mean can hide a method that improves ordinary days but fails on the peak days Botie most cares about.

Origins and horizons can overlap, so errors are not generally independent. A simple standard error treating every cell as an unrelated observation can be misleading. Report the evaluation design and use an uncertainty method compatible with its dependence.

title: Trying an Action Before Knowing Its Value
blurb: Botie can choose a watering schedule, but sees the result only for the schedule he actually tries. He must balance using his current favourite with learning about alternatives.
openingTitle: Should Botie Keep Using the Schedule That Worked Once?
opening: Two watering schedules are available. The first produced a good result yesterday, while the second has barely been tried. Repeating the first might work well today, but it leaves Botie uncertain about whether the second is better.

This is a decision that also collects information. We will first treat each trial as independent of later conditions, then learn how to update an action's estimated reward and occasionally explore another action.

history.title: Experiments Whose Choices Affect What We Learn

sources.title: Robbins: Some Aspects of the Sequential Design of Experiments (1952)

blocks: Robbins's 1952 work on sequential experimental design helped formalise problems in which the next experiment depends on what earlier experiments revealed. Sampling a treatment gathers information, but the chosen treatment also determines the outcome received during that trial.

A multi-armed bandit isolates this exploration problem. Our schedules and numerical rewards are invented. Real watering changes future soil conditions, so the independent-trial bandit is only an initial simplification.

intuition.title: Start with unequal experience
intuition.explanation: One action has several observed outcomes and another has only one. Their sample means do not carry equal amounts of evidence.

intuition.title: Try the uncertain action
intuition.explanation: If B next earns three, its apparent advantage changes. Update B using B's own observations.

intuition.title: Reserve some choices for learning
intuition.explanation: An epsilon-greedy policy usually chooses a highest estimated value, but sometimes samples uniformly across actions.

parts.title: 1. Define the Feedback We Receive
paragraphs: An action is one available choice. A reward is the numerical feedback after taking it. An action-value estimate is our current estimate of its expected reward. We observe feedback for the action selected, not the unrealised alternatives.

A reward must describe the objective we intend to optimise. A signal based only on immediate water savings could reward starving plants. In this bandit lesson, rewards are supplied synthetic measurements rather than a recommendation for greenhouse control.
interpretation: The simplified environment has no state transition affecting future trials.

parts.title: 2. Update an Average Without Storing Every Reward
paragraphs: Keep a separate count and reward estimate for each schedule. When Botie tries one schedule, only that schedule has gained a new observation. Increase its count and move its mean toward the new reward by the reciprocal of the updated count.
For the first trial, that sets the estimate to the observed reward. Updating the untried schedule too would give it credit or blame for an outcome we never observed under that choice.
parts.calculation:
Old estimate = 7; previous count = 1; new reward = 3
New count = 2
New estimate = 7 + (3 - 7) / 2 = 5
interpretation: This update equals the arithmetic mean of that action's observed rewards.

parts.title: 3. Separate Exploration From Greedy Choice
paragraphs: A greedy policy chooses an action with a highest estimated value. An epsilon-greedy policy explores with probability epsilon and otherwise chooses greedily. Here exploration samples uniformly from all actions, including a greedy one.
With one unique greedy action, it can therefore be selected through either branch. Define tie handling and seed the generator when comparing runs.
parts.calculation:
Two actions; epsilon = 0.2
Greedy action probability = 0.8 + 0.2 / 2 = 0.9
Other action probability = 0.2 / 2 = 0.1
interpretation: Exploration probability is not the same as the probability of choosing a non-greedy action.

examples.title: Update the estimate of one tried action
paragraphs: One schedule has been tried three times and averaged four units of reward. Its next observed reward is eight. We revise that schedule's estimate without claiming to have learned anything new about the other schedule.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
old_count = 3
old_mean = 4.0
reward = 8.0
new_count = old_count + 1
correction = (reward - old_mean) / new_count
print(new_count)
print(old_mean + correction)
interpretation: The new observation receives one quarter of the updated average. Practice adds the bookkeeping needed to select and update one entry in arrays of actions.

parts.title: 4. Evaluate a Sequence of Decisions
paragraphs: A lucky first observation can mislead a greedy learner. Compare policies over repeated seeded simulations and inspect both collected reward and action counts. Keep test conditions separate from the random sequence used to choose settings.
Sample averages assume a stable reward distribution for each action. In a changing environment, a fixed update rate may track recent rewards better, but it no longer equals the full historical mean.
interpretation: Botie's construction performs one correctly attributed update. The next lesson adds a state so actions can affect what happens afterward.

parts.title: 5. Only the Chosen Action Supplies a Reward
paragraphs: A bandit learner chooses one schedule and sees its result. It cannot update the unchosen schedule with the reward it imagines that schedule would have produced. In a simulation, the evaluator may know both reward distributions, but the agent still receives only its chosen outcome.

Keep counts and value estimates for every action. An epsilon-greedy choice sometimes samples an action to gather information; otherwise it chooses an action with the largest current estimate. Define a tie rule so initial behaviour is understandable.

parts.title: 6. Update Only the Action That Was Tried
paragraphs: The incremental mean needs the selected action's own count. A global step count gives the wrong denominator when actions have been tried different numbers of times.
This trace supplies the chosen actions and rewards, isolating the estimate update from the selection policy. The complete experiment adds a policy before each feedback event.

examples.title: Retain separate experience for two schedules
paragraphs: The first schedule is tried twice and the second once.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
count = np.zeros(2, dtype=int)
value = np.zeros(2)
for action, reward in [(0,1.), (1,4.), (0,3.)]:
    count[action] += 1
    value[action] += (reward-value[action])/count[action]
print(count.tolist())
print(value.tolist())
interpretation: The second schedule has a larger estimate but less evidence. Greedy selection alone does not account for that uncertainty.

parts.title: 7. One Lucky Reward Does Not Establish a Better Policy
paragraphs: Compare policies over complete sequences and repeated seeded environments. Keep the reward process stationary if that is the assumption being tested; a changing process requires a learner that can forget outdated evidence.

In a simulator with known expected rewards, expected regret compares the chosen action's expectation with the best available expectation. Realised reward remains noisy. Do not give the agent the simulator's hidden best action merely because the evaluator can use it.

quiz.prompt: What is B's updated sample mean?
quiz.because: Combine both of B's observations with equal weight.

title: Describing What an Action Changes
blurb: Watering changes the greenhouse Botie will face tomorrow. A state, an action, and a transition model let us describe that consequence before choosing a policy.
openingTitle: The Greenhouse Remembers What Botie Did Yesterday
opening: A schedule's value depends on the soil. Watering a dry tray may help, while watering an already wet tray may waste water. The same action cannot be evaluated sensibly without describing the situation in which it is taken.

Let's describe the situations the greenhouse can be in. For each state, we need to know which actions Botie can take and what might happen after each action. The next state may be uncertain, so we will record transition probabilities. Along with the reward rule, these give us a small Markov decision process to investigate.

history.title: Planning With a State That Changes After Each Choice

sources.title: Bellman: The Theory of Dynamic Programming (1954)
Stanford CS234: Tabular Decision Processes and Learning

blocks: Dynamic programming developed a way to solve multistage decisions by describing the current situation and the remaining problem. Bellman's work in the 1950s made this recursive view central to sequential planning.

A Markov decision process supplies states, actions, transitions, and rewards. Our dry-or-moist greenhouse is a deliberately simplified model. Its value is that every transition can be inspected, not that two labels fully describe soil behaviour.

intuition.title: Describe the situation
intuition.explanation: Use two state IDs with explicit meanings.

intuition.title: Condition the next-state probabilities on an action
intuition.explanation: From dry soil, watering is assumed to reach moist soil more often than waiting.

intuition.title: Keep value separate from probability
intuition.explanation: If the supplied next-state values are zero and ten, weight those values by the transition probabilities.

parts.title: 1. Choose a State That Contains the Needed Information
paragraphs: A state is the information used to predict the consequences of an action. The Markov assumption says that, given the current state and action, earlier history adds no further information about the next transition and reward distribution.

This is a modelling assumption, not a property guaranteed by giving a variable the name state. If two trays have the same moisture label but different root conditions that affect outcomes, our state may omit important information.
interpretation: Partial observations may require remembering history or maintaining a belief over hidden states.

parts.title: 2. Describe Actions, Rewards, and Transition Rows
paragraphs: An action is a choice available in a state. A transition row gives probabilities for the possible next states after that choice. Entries must be non-negative and sum to one. A reward describes immediate feedback, which may depend on the transition as well.
Keep the next-state order fixed across transition rows and value vectors. Multiplying a probability by the wrong state's value can produce a plausible but meaningless result.
parts.calculation:
Next states: [dry, moist]
P(next | dry, water) = [0.1,0.9]
P(next | dry, wait) = [0.8,0.2]
interpretation: The transition probabilities are supplied assumptions in this lesson, not estimated greenhouse measurements.

parts.title: 3. A Policy Connects States to Choices
paragraphs: A deterministic policy selects one action in each state. A stochastic policy assigns action probabilities. Either can behave differently in dry and moist states.
A transition model describes what the environment does after an action; a policy describes which action the agent chooses. Do not confuse the two probability tables.
parts.calculation:
Example policy:
if dry: water
if moist: wait
interpretation: The policy can be evaluated under the transition model even before learning a policy from experience.

examples.title: Account for one action's possible next states
paragraphs: Suppose waiting leaves the bed dry with probability three quarters and moist otherwise. The two state values describe what those consequences are worth.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
transition = np.array([0.75, 0.25])
state_values = np.array([0., 8.])
contributions = transition * state_values
print(contributions.tolist())
print(float(contributions.sum()))
interpretation: The expected value weights both possible outcomes. It is not a claim that the next state will have value two; this environment only has the two supplied states.

parts.title: 4. Calculate an Expected Next-State Value
paragraphs: Multiply each possible next state's supplied value by its transition probability, then add. This is an expectation over possible outcomes, not a prediction that one trial will return the average outcome.
A complete action comparison adds immediate expected reward and an appropriate future discount. We will introduce that accumulation next; Botie's construction here isolates the expectation step.
parts.calculation:
Expected next value after watering
= 0.1 × 0 + 0.9 × 10
= 9
interpretation: A single transition still lands in one state. Repeated trials need not equal the expectation exactly.

parts.title: 5. The Same Observation Can Hide Different Situations
paragraphs: A dry-soil reading can occur immediately after a sensor fault or after several days without water. If those situations have different next outcomes under the same action, the reading alone may not supply a useful Markov state.

Add relevant history or maintain a belief over hidden conditions when needed. The Markov assumption says the chosen state contains the information needed for predicting the next transition. Naming an array state does not make that assumption true.

parts.title: 6. Check That Each Action Defines a Distribution
paragraphs: For each current state and action, the next-state probabilities should be nonnegative and sum to one. Their positions must refer to the same state vocabulary throughout the model.

An expected-value calculation averages across those outcomes. A simulated transition instead draws one outcome from that distribution. Confusing the two can produce a learner that experiences averaged states that do not actually exist.

examples.title: Calculate the distribution and its expected continuation
paragraphs: The two entries are dry and moist. This row describes the result of watering a dry tray.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
probability = np.array([.2,.8])
next_value = np.array([-2.,3.])
print(bool((probability >= 0).all() and np.isclose(probability.sum(), 1)))
print(round(float(probability@next_value), 3))
interpretation: The expected value is two, but the next state is still either dry or moist. It is not a new state halfway between them.

quiz.prompt: What is the expected next-state value?
quiz.because: Weight each state's value by its matching probability.

given.data: Next-state order: [dry,moist]. Probabilities after watering: [0.1,0.9]. Values: [0,10].

quiz.prompt: These tables describe different choices in the interaction.
quiz.because: One describes the agent and the other the environment.

given.data: A policy gives probabilities of actions in a state; a transition model gives probabilities of next states after an action.

quiz.prompt: What needs correction?
options: The row does not sum to one
Next-state values must sum to one
quiz.because: Mutually exclusive exhaustive next-state outcomes require a total probability of one.

quiz.prompt: The moisture-only state is guaranteed to satisfy the Markov assumption.
quiz.because: The omitted history-relevant information can invalidate that assumption.

title: Valuing Rewards That Arrive Later
blurb: An action can cost water now and help a plant later. A return combines a sequence of rewards so Botie can compare more than the immediate outcome.
openingTitle: Would Botie Reject a Useful Action Because It Costs Something Now?
opening: Watering costs resources immediately, while healthier growth appears later. If Botie judges only the immediate reward, the useful action can look worse than doing nothing.

We need a way to judge an action using rewards that arrive later too. A return combines rewards over time. Discounting controls how much a delayed reward contributes compared with an immediate one. Before calculating it, we should ask whether that preference matches the job we want Botie to do.

history.title: Connecting Immediate Feedback to Later Outcomes

sources.title: Sutton: Learning to Predict by the Methods of Temporal Differences (1988)
Stanford CS234: Tabular Decision Processes and Learning

blocks: Sequential prediction needed to account for outcomes that arrive after several intermediate steps. Sutton's 1988 work developed temporal-difference learning, where later predictions help improve earlier predictions before a final outcome is available.

Before using that update, we need to define the quantity predicted. A discounted return combines future rewards with a stated time convention. Our short watering episode makes the accumulation explicit.

intuition.title: Separate the steps
intuition.explanation: The action costs one unit now and leads to a later reward in this invented completed episode.

intuition.title: Choose the discount
intuition.explanation: With gamma one half, later contributions receive successively smaller weights.

intuition.title: Combine the contributions
intuition.explanation: The discounted return is zero under this particular weighting, even though the undiscounted total is positive.

parts.title: 1. Define the Reward Sequence Before Adding It
paragraphs: An episode is a sequence that ends at a terminal condition. Its return starts with the reward received after the current action. In our arrays, the first entry is that immediate reward, not a reward from before the decision.
The reward design and episode boundary affect what is optimised. Cutting off a simulation for convenience is not necessarily the same as reaching a genuine terminal state.
parts.calculation: Rewards after the current action: r[0], r[1], r[2], ...
interpretation: State clearly whether the final reward has already been included.

parts.title: 2. Apply One Discount for Each Additional Delay
paragraphs: Gamma controls the weight retained per time step. Values between zero and one emphasise earlier rewards; gamma zero ignores later rewards. Gamma one gives an undiscounted sum for a finite episode.

Discounting can encode a preference over delay and helps define finite returns in continuing problems under suitable conditions. It is not universally the physical probability that a plant survives each day.
interpretation: Gamma controls how much future rewards contribute to the return. Changing it can change which behaviour the agent prefers.

parts.title: 3. Work Backward Through a Completed Episode
paragraphs: The return at a position equals its immediate reward plus gamma times the return beginning at the next position. At the end of a completed finite episode, there is no remaining reward.

A backward loop calculates every position's return without recomputing every suffix separately. These are realised returns from one episode; a value function predicts their expectation under a policy.
parts.calculation:
G[t] = r[t] + gamma × G[t+1]
Beyond the terminal step: G = 0
interpretation: This recurrence is the connection to the Bellman calculations in the next lesson.

examples.title: See each reward's contribution before adding
paragraphs: These rewards arrive now, one step later and two steps later. Give each delay its own power of the discount before forming the return from the start.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rewards = np.array([2., 0., 8.])
gamma = 0.5
weights = gamma ** np.arange(len(rewards))
contributions = weights * rewards
print(weights.tolist())
print(contributions.tolist())
print(float(contributions.sum()))
interpretation: The distant reward contributes less because it is delayed twice. The challenge asks for the return starting at every position, which is easier to calculate backwards.

parts.title: 4. Separate Observed Returns From Estimated Values
paragraphs: Two episodes under the same policy can produce different returns because transitions and rewards may be random. A single successful episode does not establish that a policy has high expected value.

Compare policies across repeated trials or a known transition model, keeping the reward definition and discount fixed. Botie's construction combines a supplied episode's rewards with its discount weights.
interpretation: The workshop reports a realised discounted return. It neither learns a policy nor estimates an expectation from one trace.

parts.title: 5. Calculate a Return for Every Decision in the Episode
paragraphs: The first action needs all later rewards, but later actions need only their remaining suffix. Starting from the episode's end lets us reuse the return already calculated for the next position.
The result contains one return per action time. It is not one reward copied onto every decision, and it still reflects the actions actually taken later in that episode.

examples.title: Propagate the harvest reward backward
paragraphs: The episode pays two small costs before a final benefit. Discount is one half.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rewards = np.array([-1., -1., 8.])
returns = np.zeros_like(rewards)
future = 0.
for t in range(len(rewards)-1, -1, -1):
    future = rewards[t] + .5*future
    returns[t] = future
print(returns.tolist())
interpretation: The first decision includes both later costs and benefits at their respective delays.

parts.title: 6. A Time Limit Is Not Always the End of the Task
paragraphs: A true terminal state has no future reward under the task definition. A training rollout that stops because a time limit was reached may still represent an ongoing process. Setting the continuation to zero then changes the target.

For a continuing task, a truncated rollout can use an estimated value at its final state. State clearly whether the time limit is part of the environment's objective or merely a sampling limit. This distinction carries directly into temporal-difference targets.

parts.title: 7. Observed Returns Can Vary under the Same Policy
paragraphs: Different transitions and action samples can produce different returns from the same state. Averaging repeated returns estimates a policy value under those conditions, but long episodes can have substantial variability.

Bootstrapped methods use a current value estimate for part of the future, trading some dependence on that estimate for shorter sampled targets. Neither the discounted sum nor one successful episode establishes that a policy is optimal.

quiz.prompt: Only the immediate reward contributes to the return.
quiz.because: Every later reward is multiplied by a zero discount power.

quiz.prompt: What continuation return belongs beyond its terminal step?

given.data: A completed finite episode ends. No additional rewards follow.

quiz.prompt: Its expected return is necessarily ten.
quiz.because: An expectation concerns the distribution of possible runs, not a single outcome.

practice.title: Can you distinguish a terminal end from a truncated rollout?
practice.question: Can you distinguish a terminal end from a truncated rollout?
task: Write returns_from(rewards, discount, continuation=0). rewards is a finite one-dimensional sequence; discount is finite and between zero and one; continuation is a finite estimate immediately after the last reward. Return one discounted return per reward without changing rewards.

Use continuation zero for a true terminal end. A truncated continuing rollout may supply a nonzero continuation. Empty rewards return an empty array. Raise ValueError for invalid inputs. Print both demonstration paths.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def returns_from(rewards, discount, continuation=0):
    # Write the procedure here.
    raise NotImplementedError

print(returns_from([1,2], .5).tolist())
print(returns_from([1,2], .5, 4).tolist())
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def returns_from(rewards, discount, continuation=0):
    rewards = np.asarray(rewards, dtype=float)
    if rewards.ndim != 1 or not np.isfinite(rewards).all() or not np.isfinite(discount) or not 0 <= discount <= 1 or not np.isfinite(continuation):
        raise ValueError('Invalid return inputs')
    result = np.empty_like(rewards)
    future = float(continuation)
    for t in range(len(rewards)-1,-1,-1):
        future = rewards[t] + discount*future
        result[t] = future
    return result

title: Planning One Step, Then the Remaining Journey
blurb: A long sequence of choices is difficult to compare directly. We can combine the reward from one action with the value of the state it leaves behind, then improve those estimates repeatedly.
openingTitle: Can Botie Plan Without Listing Every Possible Future?
opening: Each watering choice can lead to several future states, each with its own choices. Listing every complete future quickly becomes unwieldy. But many different paths can lead back to the same state.

We can keep one estimate for the remaining value of each state. Compare actions using their immediate rewards and those estimates, then update the state values and repeat. This reuses the same subproblem wherever it occurs.

history.title: Reusing the Remaining Decision Problem

sources.title: Bellman: The Theory of Dynamic Programming (1954)
Stanford CS234: Tabular Decision Processes and Learning

blocks: Bellman's dynamic-programming approach expressed a multistage problem through an immediate choice and the problem remaining afterward. A state's value summarises that remaining problem, avoiding a separate calculation for every history that reaches it.
Value iteration repeatedly applies an optimality update under a known model. Our finite teaching environment separates this planning calculation from learning an unknown model through interaction.

intuition.title: Start with values for the remaining problem
intuition.explanation: Suppose the possible next states currently have estimated values two and six.

intuition.title: Compare immediate and later contributions
intuition.explanation: One action gives a larger immediate reward but a worse continuation.

intuition.title: Choose using the complete action score
intuition.explanation: The first action has the higher complete score at this discount, even though the second leads to a state with a larger supplied value.

parts.title: 1. Calculate an Action Value From a Supplied Model
paragraphs: For each action, combine expected immediate reward with the discounted expectation of the next state's value. A transition row averages over next states; the discount then scales the continuation.
Here rewards are already expected immediate rewards for each state-action pair. If a reward depends on the next state, its expectation must also be calculated under that transition row.
parts.calculation: Q(s,a) = expected_reward(s,a) + gamma × sum_next P(next|s,a) V(next)
interpretation: The value vector belongs to the next-state axis, not the action axis.

parts.title: 2. Distinguish Evaluating a Policy From Improving It
paragraphs: Suppose we already have a policy. To estimate how it behaves, we average action values using the probabilities with which that policy chooses actions. Value iteration asks a different question: which action currently has the greatest estimated value in this state?

That maximum is the optimality update we will use. Early estimates can be inaccurate, so choosing their current best action does not mean we have already found the optimal policy. We repeat the updates and examine convergence under the model's assumptions.
parts.calculation:
Fixed policy: V_new(s) = sum_a policy(a|s) Q(s,a)
Optimality update: V_new(s) = max_a Q(s,a)
interpretation: Do not substitute a maximum into a calculation claimed to evaluate a fixed non-greedy policy.

parts.title: 3. Repeat With a Consistent Set of Old Values
paragraphs: In synchronous value iteration, calculate every new state value from the same old vector. Only replace the vector after the complete sweep. Reusing already updated entries within a sweep is a different update schedule.
Terminal states have no continuation and stay at their defined terminal value, typically zero after the terminal reward is counted. Stop using a chosen change tolerance or iteration budget.
parts.calculation:
V_old → all action scores → V_new
change = max(abs(V_new - V_old))
interpretation: A finite discounted problem with bounded rewards has useful convergence guarantees, but floating-point tolerance is still a practical stopping decision.

examples.title: Combine a payment now with a continuation later
paragraphs: Compare two actions whose next states are known here. One pays immediately but has little continuation value; the other pays nothing now and reaches a more useful state.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
immediate = np.array([2., 0.])
continuation = np.array([1., 8.])
gamma = 0.5
scores = immediate + gamma * continuation
print(scores.tolist())
print(int(np.argmax(scores)))
interpretation: The second action wins after including the continuation. Practice replaces these supplied next-state values with expectations under a transition model.

parts.title: 4. Inspect the Policy and the Model Assumptions
paragraphs: After updating values, choose a highest-scoring action in each state. Check the resulting actions, terminal handling, and reward accounting in simple states with known answers.

A perfectly solved inaccurate model can still produce a poor real policy. Botie's workshop calculates action scores for one state; the Python example repeats that principle in a complete two-state model.
interpretation: Planning assumes transitions and rewards are known. The next lesson replaces a model expectation with sampled experience.

parts.title: 5. One Sweep Uses One Consistent Old Value Table
paragraphs: For each state, calculate the expected reward plus discounted continuation for every action, then retain the best action value. A synchronous sweep reads all continuations from the old table and writes a new table.

Updating entries in place creates a different update schedule. It can still be a useful algorithm, but its intermediate values should not be compared as though it performed the same synchronous sweep.

parts.title: 6. Iterate a Small Known Model to a Stable Decision
paragraphs: This two-state model gives Botie an action that stays where he is and an action that moves to the other state. Rewards belong to state-action pairs, and transitions are deterministic here.
Repeat until the largest table change is small or an explicit iteration limit is reached. Then extract the greedy action from the converged action values.

examples.title: Plan before collecting experience
paragraphs: Rows are states and columns are actions. The transition table stores the next-state index.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
reward = np.array([[0.,1.],[2.,0.]])
next_state = np.array([[0,1],[1,0]])
value = np.zeros(2)
for _ in range(1000):
    action_value = reward + .5*value[next_state]
    updated = action_value.max(axis=1)
    change = np.max(np.abs(updated-value))
    value = updated
    if change < 1e-10:
        break
policy = (reward + .5*value[next_state]).argmax(axis=1)
print(np.round(value, 4).tolist())
print(policy.tolist())
interpretation: The plan moves from state zero to state one, then takes the rewarding stay action there. The result relies on knowing the supplied transition and reward model.

parts.title: 7. A Stable Calculation Can Plan for the Wrong Greenhouse
paragraphs: For a finite discounted model with valid probabilities and discount below one, Bellman optimality updates contract differences between value tables. This supports convergence of the planning calculation.

It does not establish that the model accurately describes the greenhouse. A missing action cost or incorrect transition probability can produce a precisely computed but poor real policy. Compare simulated policy behaviour with observed transitions and test sensitivity to uncertain model entries.
