title: Investigate a Sensor Before Calling It Faulty
blurb: Fit a reference from earlier readings, select an alert rule on validation records, and evaluate that fixed rule on later labelled cases.
openingTitle: Which Readings Should Botie Send for Inspection?
opening: Botie cannot ask a technician to inspect every pressure reading. He needs a small, understandable alert procedure and an honest estimate of how often it sends the wrong cases for review.

We will build the alert procedure from the readings through to the decision to request an inspection. Along the way, we need a fitted reference and a way to select a threshold without using the final test answers. The records are small and synthetic so we can check those choices before trying the procedure on a larger dataset.

history.title: From Robust Estimates to an Investigation Procedure

sources.title: Huber: Robust Estimation of a Location Parameter
Breck and colleagues: The ML Test Score

blocks: Robust estimation addresses how unusual observations affect a reference. Production testing adds another concern: what happens when that reference is used repeatedly on new records.

This project combines those concerns in a teaching workflow. An alert is a request to investigate, while a fault label comes from a separate inspection. Keeping those meanings distinct prevents the detector from becoming its own source of truth.

quiz.prompt: What is its total cost?
quiz.because: Apply the two costs separately.

given.data: False alert cost 1, missed fault cost 5. A rule has two false alerts and one miss.

quiz.prompt: The test remains untouched final evaluation.
quiz.because: It now influences selection.

given.data: Test labels are used to pick a threshold after validation.

quiz.prompt: Should it alert?
options: Only if test labels say fault
quiz.because: Its score equals the threshold.

given.data: Median=10, MAD=1, threshold=4 with strict greater-than. Reading=14.

quiz.prompt: Estimating missed faults requires additional information.
quiz.because: Unalerted outcomes are selectively unobserved.

given.data: Only alerted records are ever inspected.

build.title: Build the inspection rule
build.problem: Botie has retained reference values and a validation-selected threshold.
build.challenge: Subtract the retained centre, divide absolute differences by retained MAD, and alert strictly above the fixed threshold.
build.why: The deployed rule reuses fitting and selection decisions instead of relearning from the test window.
build.limitation: This is an alert procedure. Fault status comes from independent inspection, not the alert itself.

intuition.title: Fit only the reference window
intuition.explanation: Retain its centre and spread.

intuition.title: Choose a rule on validation
intuition.explanation: Missed faults cost more in this toy decision.

intuition.title: Evaluate once on later records
intuition.explanation: Freeze the threshold before reading test labels.

parts.title: 1. Write the Inspection Question
paragraphs: The outcome is whether a reading corresponds to a confirmed fault under the inspection procedure. The action is sending a case for review. For this project, a false alert costs one unit and a missed fault costs five units.
These are invented decision costs. In practice they should reflect the burden and consequences of investigation. Keep measurement units and operating mode consistent across the three windows.
interpretation: A score alone does not choose the right operational threshold.

parts.title: 2. Fit a Simple Reference and Baseline
paragraphs: Use only the earlier reference values to fit median and raw MAD. Retain both values. The no-alert baseline misses all faults but creates no investigations, so it provides a useful cost comparison.
Check that the MAD is positive. If it is zero, stop and choose a documented reference policy before proceeding. Do not replace it using test data.
parts.calculation:
Reference median = 10; raw MAD = 1
Validation scores for [10,13,15] = [0,3,5]
interpretation: The raw MAD convention must remain identical in every window.

parts.title: 3. Choose Among Declared Thresholds
paragraphs: Evaluate thresholds two and four on validation, using a strict greater-than comparison. Count false alerts and missed faults separately, multiply by their costs, and choose the smaller total. Use the first threshold on a tie.
Do not add more threshold candidates after inspecting the test outcomes. That would turn the final test into another selection set.
parts.calculation:
Threshold 2: one false alert, zero missed faults; cost = 1
Threshold 4: zero false alerts, zero missed faults; cost = 0
Selected threshold = 4
interpretation: A perfect result on three validation records is weak evidence; it is only enough to illustrate selection.

examples.title: Apply a rule whose fitting decisions have already been made
paragraphs: For this illustration, the reference centre, raw MAD and alert threshold are already fixed. Score new readings without allowing them to move the reference.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
readings = np.array([8., 10., 16.])
saved_centre, saved_mad = 10.0, 2.0
threshold = 2.0
scores = np.abs(readings - saved_centre) / saved_mad
print(scores.tolist())
print((scores > threshold).tolist())
interpretation: Only the last reading exceeds the chosen threshold. The project challenge goes back a step: fit the reference and select a threshold using validation data, then freeze those decisions.

parts.title: 4. Evaluate the Frozen Procedure
paragraphs: Score the later test values using the same centre and MAD. Apply the selected threshold once, then compute alerts and costs from the held-out labels. Preserve per-record results so aggregate performance can be inspected.
Report the tiny sample size, operating conditions, and synthetic nature of this exercise. Do not treat its error rate as a production guarantee.
parts.calculation:
Test scores = [1,4,6]
With score > 4: alerts = [False,False,True]
Test cost = 0
interpretation: The reading exactly at the threshold does not alert.

parts.title: 5. Prepare an Investigation Record
paragraphs: For each alert, retain the original reading, reference version, score, threshold, and eventual inspection result. Later revisions can then distinguish a model change from a changed label or sensor repair.
Inspect missed cases too. A review process that labels only alerts cannot directly measure how many unalerted faults occurred without additional sampling.
interpretation: Your deliverable is a reproducible procedure and an evaluation record, not simply a fitted detector.

parts.title: 6. Keep a Record of the Decision, Then Add the Inspection
paragraphs: A detector produces an alert before a person knows whether the sensor failed. Give every reading a stable identifier and store its value, score, threshold, rule version and decision. Add the inspection result later, rather than overwriting the original decision.

An uninspected reading does not mean a healthy sensor. If inspectors only examine alerts, measured precision may be available while missed failures remain unknown. Sample some non-alerts for inspection when the project needs a recall estimate. Keep these two sources of evidence separate in the report.

parts.title: 7. Freeze the Reference While Scoring New Batches
paragraphs: The reference median and median absolute deviation describe the period we chose as normal. A new extreme reading must not change those numbers while it is being scored. Otherwise, the reading can move its own threshold.

A changed production process may eventually justify a new reference period, but inspect the shift first. Store the new rule with a new version and compare its decisions with the previous one. A zero reference deviation needs an explicit policy; our function rejects it instead of dividing by zero or inventing a tolerance.

parts.title: 8. Make an Inspection Report Reproducible
paragraphs: Save the frozen rule with the values, scores and alert flags. A second program should be able to reproduce every decision using only that report. Include the strict comparison convention: a score equal to the threshold is not an alert here.

Try a fresh batch with one enormous reading. Scores for the unchanged readings should stay the same. Then try a genuinely different reference rule and explain which decisions change. The report is an inspectable record of a rule, not proof that every alert was a real fault.

practice.title: Can you choose an alert threshold using validation only?
practice.question: Can you choose an alert threshold using validation only?
task: Fit reference median and raw MAD. Evaluate thresholds [2,4] with cost FP+5*FN, strict comparison, first tie wins. Print validation costs and chosen threshold.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
reference = np.array([8.,9.,10.,11.,12.])
validation = np.array([10.,13.,15.])
fault = np.array([0,0,1],dtype=bool)
thresholds = np.array([2.,4.])
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
reference = np.array([8.,9.,10.,11.,12.])
validation = np.array([10.,13.,15.])
fault = np.array([0,0,1],dtype=bool)
thresholds = np.array([2.,4.])
centre = np.median(reference)
mad = np.median(np.abs(reference-centre))
scores = np.abs(validation-centre)/mad
costs = []
for threshold in thresholds:
    alert = scores>threshold
    costs.append(int(np.sum(alert & ~fault)+5*np.sum(~alert & fault)))
print(costs)
print(float(thresholds[np.argmin(costs)]))
hints: Fit centre and spread before looking at validation labels.
Choose by cost, not by the number of alerts alone.

practice.title: Can you score fresh readings without moving the reference?
practice.question: Can you score fresh readings without moving the reference?
task: Implement score_alerts(values, rule), returning NumPy arrays (scores, alerts). The dictionary rule supplies centre, mad and threshold. Scores are absolute distances from centre divided by mad; alerts use a strict greater-than comparison.

Require a finite one-dimensional input, finite rule values, positive mad and nonnegative threshold. Raise ValueError otherwise. Do not refit the reference from values. Run the supplied report code and download the result.
practice.starter:
import json
import numpy as np

def score_alerts(values, rule):
    # Write the procedure here.
    raise NotImplementedError

values=[9,14,16,17]
rule={'version':1,'centre':10,'mad':1,'threshold':4}
scores,alerts=score_alerts(values,rule)
report_json=json.dumps({'rule':rule,'values':values,'scores':scores.tolist(),'alerts':alerts.tolist()},indent=2)

print(alerts.tolist())
practice.solution:
import json
import numpy as np

def score_alerts(values, rule):
    values=np.asarray(values,dtype=float)
    centre,mad,threshold=[float(rule[k]) for k in ['centre','mad','threshold']]
    if values.ndim!=1 or not np.isfinite(values).all() or not np.isfinite([centre,mad,threshold]).all() or mad<=0 or threshold<0:
        raise ValueError('Invalid readings or reference rule')
    scores=np.abs(values-centre)/mad
    return scores,scores>threshold

values=[9,14,16,17]
rule={'version':1,'centre':10,'mad':1,'threshold':4}
scores,alerts=score_alerts(values,rule)
report_json=json.dumps({'rule':rule,'values':values,'scores':scores.tolist(),'alerts':alerts.tolist()},indent=2)
print(scores.tolist())
print(alerts.tolist())
hints: Read centre and mad from the dictionary. Computing either from this batch would change the detector you are evaluating.
Compare the entire score array with the threshold. NumPy returns one Boolean for each reading.

tests.name: A different reference and boundary give the stated decisions

np.testing.assert_allclose(scores,[2,0,3])
np.testing.assert_array_equal(alerts,[False,False,True])

title: Forecast Tomorrow’s Water Demand Without Seeing Tomorrow
blurb: Build lagged inputs, compare an autoregressive model with persistence, and evaluate both through a sequence of later forecast origins.
openingTitle: How Much Water Should Botie Prepare for the Next Day?
opening: Botie needs a forecast before tomorrow’s water demand is known. A model that sees tomorrow while constructing today’s input can look excellent in a notebook and be impossible to use.

We will replay the forecast at successive dates. At each date, the model gets only the history available then. A persistence forecast gives us a simple comparison for the fitted autoregression. After saving both predictions, we can look at the later demand and measure their errors on the same target.

history.title: Evaluating Predictions at the Time They Could Have Been Made

sources.title: Hyndman and Athanasopoulos: Forecasting Principles and Practice

blocks: Forecast evaluation asks what information would have been available at each prediction time. Rolling-origin evaluation recreates that boundary repeatedly rather than randomly mixing earlier and later observations.
Our demand sequence is synthetic and intentionally simple. It provides a testable implementation of the boundary, not evidence that a one-lag linear model is sufficient for real water planning.

quiz.prompt: Which records may be used for fitting at that origin?
options: Any randomly shuffled subset of future days
quiz.because: The target is not yet available.

given.data: Forecast target is day 6; days 1 to 5 are available.

quiz.prompt: The chronological loop alone removes that leakage.
quiz.because: Preparation has already seen the future.

given.data: A scaler is fitted on the full series before rolling evaluation.

quiz.prompt: What is MAE?
quiz.because: Both absolute errors equal two.

given.data: Predictions [10,12], actual [12,14].

quiz.prompt: That does not establish that it handles real seasonal demand.
quiz.because: The example tests implementation, not broad empirical performance.

given.data: The autoregression fits this synthetic trend perfectly.

build.title: Compare forecasts on the same later days
build.problem: Botie supplies predictions from several procedures, with one procedure per row, and matching later outcomes.
build.challenge: Subtract the same actual vector from every forecast row, take absolute errors, and average within each procedure.
build.why: Matching targets makes the comparison reflect forecast errors rather than different evaluation days.
build.limitation: Forecasts must be stored before targets are observed. This workshop evaluates supplied predictions; fitting happens in the project code.

intuition.title: Stop the data at the origin
intuition.explanation: Only the first five observations are available.

intuition.title: Fit on earlier-to-later pairs
intuition.explanation: A lagged input predicts the next observed value.

intuition.title: Compare two forecasts
intuition.explanation: The model and baseline must target the same unseen day.

parts.title: 1. Specify Origin, Horizon, and Units
paragraphs: The origin is the last moment whose readings are available. The horizon is one day in this project, and each value is demand in the same units. Decide when daily totals become available; a total published late cannot be used before publication.
Use earlier origins for method selection and reserve later origins for final comparison. Do not choose model settings from the final error table.

A row is not automatically a day. Keep a date beside every measurement, then check that the dates are unique, ordered and consecutive before making lag pairs. If Tuesday is missing, the row before Wednesday is Monday; treating it as yesterday changes the question without telling the model. The calendar challenge below deliberately refuses that sequence. Repairing or imputing a missing measurement requires a separate, stated rule using only information available at the forecast origin.
interpretation: Every fitting call below receives only the prefix ending before its target.

parts.title: 2. Build a Baseline and a Small Learned Model
paragraphs: Persistence predicts the most recent observation. The autoregression fits an intercept and one lag coefficient with least squares. Its design matrix contains a constant column and earlier demand; targets contain the following demand.
Use a numerical least-squares solver rather than forming an inverse. Check whether the available pairs contain enough variation to identify both coefficients.
parts.calculation:
Training inputs = [2,4,6,8]
Training targets = [4,6,8,10]
Fitted intercept = 2; lag coefficient = 1
Next forecast = 2 + 1 × 10 = 12
interpretation: The exact fit follows from this invented sequence and should not be expected in real records.

parts.title: 3. Advance the Origin Without Borrowing the Target
paragraphs: After evaluating one prediction, the newly observed demand can enter the next origin’s history. Refit using that enlarged prefix if that is the chosen deployment procedure.
The same preprocessing, fitting, and forecast code must run at every origin. If a scaler is used, fit it within the prefix too. Store each prediction before inspecting its target.
interpretation: A chronological split alone does not prevent leakage inside feature preparation.

examples.title: Make a baseline at one forecast origin
paragraphs: The history stops before the unknown target day. Save the persistence prediction first, then compare it with the observation when it arrives.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
history = np.array([3., 6., 9., 12.])
prediction = float(history[-1])
later_observation = 15.0
print(prediction)
print(abs(later_observation - prediction))
interpretation: The increasing sequence leaves persistence behind here. A fitted alternative still needs an honest comparison across several origins, which is the work of the project challenge.

parts.title: 4. Compare Matched Errors
paragraphs: Calculate errors for both methods on the same target days. Report the individual errors as well as a mean, since one average can hide a costly shortage. Choose an error measure aligned with planning needs.
Absolute error treats overprediction and underprediction symmetrically. If water shortage costs more, evaluate a stated asymmetric decision cost rather than pretending MAE already represents it.
parts.calculation:
Targets = [12,14]
Persistence predictions = [10,12]; MAE = 2
Autoregressive predictions = [12,14]; MAE = 0
interpretation: The comparison supports only these synthetic evaluation cases.

parts.title: 5. Describe What Would Break the Procedure
paragraphs: Seasonal patterns, weather changes, demand caps, missing days, and delayed records can all violate this simple setup. Test those conditions separately and compare seasonal baselines when repetition is present.
For deployment, save schema and preparation with the chosen model and record forecast timestamps. Monitor errors after actual demand arrives, without silently changing the evaluation window.
interpretation: Explain what information the forecast could use at prediction time, show where it failed, and compare its score with the baseline. That gives someone else enough context to judge the result.

parts.title: 6. Try a Record That Does Not Follow Our Rule Exactly
paragraphs: A short, tidy record can make a fitted rule look more useful than it is. Now give Botie daily water measurements with both an upward trend and days that interrupt it. Keep the last five days for successive one-day forecasts. At each origin, train only on the prefix that would have existed then.

Compare the learned lag rule with persistence on exactly the same dates. Keep every error before taking an average. If the learned model loses, report that result. The purpose of this project is to discover whether fitting helped, not to arrange a victory for the fitted model.
parts.calculation:
Litres by day: [8,10,9,13,12,16,14,19,13,18]
First forecast: index 5, using indices 0 through 4
Next forecast: index 6, using indices 0 through 5
interpretation: These are invented measurements. A result on this sequence is an implementation check, not evidence of performance at a real greenhouse.

parts.title: 7. Make the Information Boundary Part of the Function
paragraphs: Write rolling_report so the function receives the complete sequence but slices a fresh training prefix inside each iteration. That makes the boundary visible in one place. Pair each previous reading with the following reading inside that prefix; never pair the final training reading with the hidden target while fitting.

Return a dictionary of named lists: origins, actual, predicted and baseline. Their matching positions describe the same forecast. Add the two mean absolute errors in the stated order. A dictionary is useful here because an unnamed tuple makes it easy to mistake actual values for predictions.

Change only the very last observation and run the function again. All predictions should stay unchanged, while the last actual value and measured error can change. This test checks the procedure rather than whether one printed answer looks plausible.

parts.title: 8. Save Enough to Reproduce a Forecast
paragraphs: For the final evaluation date, save the intercept, lag coefficient, previous-day reading and final training index. Record feature order, units and a format version alongside the parameters. These values let another program reproduce that particular forecast.

The downloadable JSON report also contains all forecast origins, predictions, targets and baseline errors. JSON represents a dictionary as named fields and NumPy arrays as ordinary lists. Convert values to Python numbers before serializing. Do not include a Python object that only the original process knows how to reconstruct.
parts.calculation: saved prediction = intercept + lag_coefficient × last_input
interpretation: This saved model was fitted before the final evaluation target. A deployment model might later be refitted on more observations; give that model a new record rather than silently replacing the evaluated one.

parts.title: 9. Decide What the Errors Tell Us to Try Next
paragraphs: Inspect the largest date-level errors. Did both rules miss a sudden change, or did the fitted rule amplify a temporary increase? A weather measurement might explain a change, but only use a weather value that would have been available when the forecast was made.

Keep a later period untouched while choosing features and settings. Repeatedly choosing whichever rule wins on these five dates turns this small evaluation into training feedback. The final report should state the time boundary, the baseline comparison and a specific next experiment, including a disappointing result when that is what the measurements show.

practice.title: Can you run a rolling-origin comparison?
practice.question: Can you run a rolling-origin comparison?
task: At origins 5 and 6, fit intercept-plus-one-lag least squares using only history before the origin. Predict that origin’s value. Print model predictions and MAEs for persistence then model, rounded to three decimals.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([2.,4.,6.,8.,10.,12.,14.])
origins = [5,6]
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
y = np.array([2.,4.,6.,8.,10.,12.,14.])
origins = [5,6]
model, baseline, actual = [], [], []
for origin in origins:
    history = y[:origin]
    X = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(history)-1),history[:-1]])
    weights = np.linalg.lstsq(X,history[1:],rcond=None)[0]
    model.append(float(np.array([1.,history[-1]]) @ weights))
    baseline.append(history[-1])
    actual.append(y[origin])
actual = np.array(actual)
print(np.round(model,3).tolist())
print(np.round([np.mean(np.abs(actual-baseline)),np.mean(np.abs(actual-model))],3).tolist())

Compare both forecasts with the same actual array.

practice.solution:
import json
import numpy as np

def rolling_report(y, start):
    y=np.asarray(y,dtype=float)
    if y.ndim!=1 or not np.isfinite(y).all():
        raise ValueError('Use a finite one-dimensional sequence')
    if not isinstance(start,(int,np.integer)) or isinstance(start,(bool,np.bool_)) or not 3<=start<len(y):
        raise ValueError('Invalid first forecast index')
    report={key:[] for key in ['origins','actual','predicted','baseline']}
    for origin in range(start,len(y)):
        history=y[:origin]
        if np.ptp(history[:-1])==0:
            raise ValueError('Lag inputs must vary')
        X=np.column_stack([np.ones(origin-1),history[:-1]])
        coefficients=np.linalg.lstsq(X,history[1:],rcond=None)[0]
        report['origins'].append(int(origin))
        report['actual'].append(float(y[origin]))
        report['predicted'].append(float(coefficients[0]+coefficients[1]*history[-1]))
        report['baseline'].append(float(history[-1]))
    actual=np.array(report['actual'])
    report['mae']=[float(np.mean(np.abs(actual-np.array(report[key])))) for key in ['baseline','predicted']]
    report['model']={'version':1,'units':'litres','feature_order':['previous_day_litres'],
        'intercept':float(coefficients[0]),'lag_coefficient':float(coefficients[1]),
        'last_input':float(history[-1]),'training_end_index':int(origin-1)}
    return report

report=rolling_report([8,10,9,13,12,16,14,19,13,18],5)
report['dataset']='Invented greenhouse water measurements'
report['horizon_days']=1
report_json=json.dumps(report,indent=2,allow_nan=False)
print(report['origins'])
print(np.round(report['mae'],3).tolist())
hints: The rows used for fitting are history[:-1] and history[1:]. The forecast input is history[-1], whose next value is still hidden.
The last saved training index is the last forecast origin minus one. The model fields must come from that last fit.

tests.name: A changed final target cannot change predictions
tests.code:
a=np.array([3.,7.,4.,9.,8.,12.,6.]); b=a.copy(); b[-1]=1000
x=rolling_report(a,3); y=rolling_report(b,3)
np.testing.assert_allclose(x['predicted'],y['predicted'])
assert x['actual'][-1]!=y['actual'][-1]

tests.name: Every forecast uses its own training prefix
tests.code:
y=np.array([2.,5.,4.,8.,6.,11.]); r=rolling_report(y,3)
assert r['origins']==[3,4,5]
for i,origin in enumerate(r['origins']):
    h=y[:origin]; slope=np.sum((h[:-1]-h[:-1].mean())*(h[1:]-h[1:].mean()))/np.sum((h[:-1]-h[:-1].mean())**2)
    expected=h[1:].mean()+slope*(h[-1]-h[:-1].mean())
    np.testing.assert_allclose(r['predicted'][i],expected)
np.testing.assert_allclose(r['mae'],[np.mean(np.abs(y[3:]-r[k])) for k in ['baseline','predicted']])

tests.name: The saved model reproduces the last reported forecast
tests.code:
r=json.loads(json.dumps(rolling_report([4,7,5,10,8,12],3)))
m=r['model']; assert m['training_end_index']==4
assert m['feature_order']==['previous_day_litres'] and m['units']=='litres'
np.testing.assert_allclose(m['intercept']+m['lag_coefficient']*m['last_input'],r['predicted'][-1])

title: Count Seeds While Keeping the Image Assumptions Visible
blurb: Turn a small tray image into a binary mask, label connected regions, and investigate when a region count stops matching the number of seeds.
openingTitle: When Does One Bright Region Mean One Seed?
opening: Botie photographs seeds on a dark tray and needs a count. Bright pixels look promising, but one seed spans several pixels, dust can look like a seed, and two touching seeds can become one region.

Let's build a count from the photograph. We will select candidate pixels, group connected ones, and examine whether a size rule separates seeds from small specks. At each stage we will keep the intermediate image visible. That lets us investigate a wrong count instead of treating the final number as sufficient evidence.

history.title: Turning Pixel Regions Into Measurable Objects

sources.title: Rosenfeld and Pfaltz: Sequential Operations in Digital Picture Processing (1966)

blocks: Early digital picture-processing work described operations that inspect pixel neighbourhoods and identify connected structures. Connectivity turns a mask of individual foreground pixels into regions that can be measured.

Our tray uses invented grayscale pixels and a simple four-neighbour rule. A region is an image structure; interpreting it as one seed requires additional assumptions about separation, lighting, and noise.

quiz.prompt: How many regions remain?
quiz.because: Count regions meeting the size rule, not pixels.

given.data: Region sizes [4,1,2,2], minimum accepted size two.

quiz.prompt: Connected-component counting can merge them into one.
quiz.because: Connectivity does not know object identity.

given.data: Two physical seeds touch in the mask.

quiz.prompt: How many regions do they form?
quiz.because: Diagonal contact is excluded.

given.data: Two foreground pixels touch only diagonally under four-neighbour connectivity.

quiz.prompt: The old minimum pixel-area threshold is guaranteed to retain the same physical objects.
quiz.because: Pixel area changes with capture scale.

given.data: The camera resolution changes.

build.title: Count candidate seeds in a tray
build.problem: Botie has a grayscale tray image and a fixed intensity and minimum-area rule.
build.challenge: Threshold the image, label four-neighbour regions, calculate each region’s size, and count those at least as large as the minimum.
build.why: Connectivity groups pixels before the area rule decides which regions to count.
build.limitation: Counts assume each accepted connected region corresponds to one seed. Touching objects and lighting changes can violate that assumption.

intuition.title: Inspect grayscale values
intuition.explanation: A bright isolated pixel may be dust, not a seed.

intuition.title: Make a foreground mask
intuition.explanation: Use a strict threshold above five.

intuition.title: Count regions that pass the size rule
intuition.explanation: Four-neighbour regions of at least two pixels remain.

parts.title: 1. Define the Capture and Label Rules
paragraphs: Assume a fixed camera, dark tray, brighter seeds, and separate seed silhouettes. Record image dtype and intensity range. Choose threshold and minimum region size on separate labelled development images.

A hand-labelled seed count is not the same as a foreground mask. Keep the evaluation label appropriate to the question: count error, segmentation overlap, and object detection each measure different things.
interpretation: These tiny arrays let us inspect mechanics before testing on real photographs.

parts.title: 2. Threshold Without Destroying the Input
paragraphs: Compare grayscale intensity with the chosen threshold to produce a Boolean foreground mask. Preserve the original image for investigating mistakes.
Uneven lighting can make a single global threshold inappropriate. Morphological cleanup can help some noise patterns but can also merge or erase seeds, so any cleanup needs its own validation.
parts.calculation:
Foreground rule: intensity > 5
Pixel 5 becomes background
Pixel 7 becomes foreground
interpretation: Threshold equality is part of the rule and belongs in the tests.

parts.title: 3. Find Connected Regions
paragraphs: We will connect pixels across shared sides: up, down, left and right. Touching only at a corner does not connect them under this four-neighbour rule. Start from an unvisited foreground pixel and use a queue or stack to find the rest of its region.

The mask tells us which pixels are foreground. A visited array prevents us from processing one twice. The queue or stack holds coordinates we still need to inspect, while a counter records the region's size. Each structure has a different job, so we will keep them separate in the implementation.
interpretation: Changing to eight-neighbour connectivity changes what counts as one region.

examples.title: Count qualifying regions after pixels have been labelled
paragraphs: Suppose the connectivity step has already given each foreground region an ID, with zero reserved for background. Count the pixels belonging to each positive ID before applying a minimum area.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
labels = np.array([[0, 1, 1], [0, 0, 2], [3, 3, 0]])
region_ids = np.unique(labels[labels > 0])
areas = np.array([np.count_nonzero(labels == region) for region in region_ids])
print(areas.tolist())
print(int(np.count_nonzero(areas >= 2)))
interpretation: There are three foreground regions, but only two meet the area rule. Practice starts from intensities and asks you to discover the connected regions yourself.

parts.title: 4. Reject Tiny Regions, Then Count
paragraphs: Filter connected regions by a minimum pixel size. In the supplied scene, the single bright pixel is removed while the three larger regions remain.

This rule can also remove a genuinely small seed. Touching seeds remain one connected component unless another separation method is added. Compare predicted and labelled counts across these failure cases.
parts.calculation:
Region sizes = [4,1,2,2]
Keep sizes >= 2
Accepted regions = 3
interpretation: The rule counts accepted regions, not physical objects by definition.

parts.title: 5. Write a Useful Failure Report
paragraphs: Evaluate on held-out tray images that vary in brightness, spacing, seed size, and dust. Record undercounts and overcounts separately and inspect masks when an error occurs.
Save threshold, connectivity, minimum area, and image preparation with the procedure. A new camera or resolution can change pixel areas even if the physical seeds are unchanged.
interpretation: The project is complete when its procedure and limits can be reproduced, including images where it fails.

parts.title: 6. Make a Test Collection That Can Disagree with Us
paragraphs: Our small pixel example checks the arithmetic. A useful counting project also needs images where the assumption of separated bright seeds is wrong. Collect dim seeds, touching seeds, dust, shadows and seeds clipped by the image boundary. Record a human count for each image and describe the counting convention for partial seeds.

Separate development images, used to choose a threshold and minimum area, from untouched evaluation images. Several crops from the same photograph should stay together so almost identical regions do not appear on both sides. Report count errors by scene condition, not only one average.

parts.title: 7. Keep the Mask and Regions Beside the Count
paragraphs: When a count is wrong, the final integer rarely tells us why. Save the threshold mask, connected-region labels and each region’s area. A missing dim seed disappears in the mask. Two touching seeds can survive the mask but share one region. Dust can appear as tiny separate regions.

Our four-neighbour search joins pixels through shared edges. It deliberately leaves diagonal contact separate. The next challenge asks you to implement that search with a stack of pixel coordinates, a Boolean visited array and a list of region sizes. Those data structures each have a distinct job.

parts.title: 8. Know When a Threshold Cannot Supply the Missing Information
paragraphs: Lowering a threshold might recover a dim seed while admitting more background. Increasing a size cutoff can remove dust while discarding a small real seed. Neither adjustment can reliably separate two objects that form one bright region.

The next experiment might change lighting, use shape information to split a region, or train a segmentation model with labelled images. Preserve the failed examples when making that decision. They explain why a more complicated method is needed and give it a fair test.

practice.title: Can you count regions without counting pixels twice?
practice.question: Can you count regions without counting pixels twice?
task: Threshold above five. Traverse four-neighbour components with a stack and visited mask. Print sorted region sizes and the count of regions with at least two pixels.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np
image = np.array([[0,9,9,0,0],[0,9,9,0,8],[0,0,0,0,0],[7,7,0,8,8]])
mask = image>5
# Write your calculation here.
practice.solution:
import numpy as np
image = np.array([[0,9,9,0,0],[0,9,9,0,8],[0,0,0,0,0],[7,7,0,8,8]])
mask = image>5
visited = np.zeros_like(mask,dtype=bool)
sizes = []
for r in range(mask.shape[0]):
    for col in range(mask.shape[1]):
        if not mask[r,col] or visited[r,col]:
            continue
        stack = [(r,col)]
        visited[r,col] = True
        size = 0
        while stack:
            a,b = stack.pop()
            size += 1
            for da,db in [(1,0),(-1,0),(0,1),(0,-1)]:
                na,nb = a+da,b+db
                if 0<=na<mask.shape[0] and 0<=nb<mask.shape[1] and mask[na,nb] and not visited[na,nb]:
                    visited[na,nb] = True
                    stack.append((na,nb))
        sizes.append(size)
print(sorted(sizes))
print(sum(size>=2 for size in sizes))
hints: Mark a pixel visited when adding it to the stack.
Check image bounds before reading a neighbour.

An empty or entirely background image returns []. Reject other dimensions or non-Boolean data with ValueError, and do not modify the input.

The supplied example converts intensities into a mask, filters regions by area and writes a report. The extra tests include diagonal contact, a ring, and empty images so memorising this example cannot pass.

practice.solution:
import json
import numpy as np

def component_sizes(mask):
    mask=np.asarray(mask)
    if mask.ndim!=2 or mask.dtype!=np.bool_:
        raise ValueError('Use a two-dimensional Boolean mask')
    seen=np.zeros_like(mask)
    rows,cols=mask.shape
    sizes=[]
    for r in range(rows):
        for c in range(cols):
            if not mask[r,c] or seen[r,c]: continue
            stack=[(r,c)]; seen[r,c]=True; size=0
            while stack:
                y,x=stack.pop(); size+=1
                for ny,nx in [(y-1,x),(y+1,x),(y,x-1),(y,x+1)]:
                    if 0<=ny<rows and 0<=nx<cols and mask[ny,nx] and not seen[ny,nx]:
                        seen[ny,nx]=True
                        stack.append((ny,nx))
            sizes.append(size)
    return sorted(sizes)

image=np.array([[0,8,8,0],[0,8,0,9],[0,0,0,0],[7,7,0,6]])
mask=image>5
areas=component_sizes(mask)
count=sum(area>=2 for area in areas)
report_json=json.dumps({'threshold':5,'minimum_area':2,'connectivity':4,'image':image.tolist(),'mask':mask.tolist(),'areas':areas,'count':count},indent=2)
print(areas)
print(count)

Finish one stack before searching for the next unvisited foreground pixel. Each completed stack gives one region size.

title: What Would This Prediction Actually Change?
blurb: A model can flag a pump that may fail, but someone still has to decide what to do. Begin with that decision and work backwards to the information it needs.
openingTitle: Botie Has an Alarm. Who Is Going to Answer It?
opening: Suppose we want to help a maintenance team find pumps that need inspection. We could start by choosing a model. But imagine that it sends the team hundreds of warnings each morning. They can inspect only a few pumps, so most of those predictions never lead to anything.

Before building that model, let's work out what the team can actually do. Who receives a warning? How much time do they have? What happens if a faulty pump is missed? Those answers give our design something to aim for.

history.title: A Requirement Has to Describe Something People Need

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: System Design Processes

blocks: Engineers working on large systems have to translate a broad request into parts that can be built and tested. NASA’s systems engineering handbook describes a progression from stakeholder expectations to technical requirements and a design. Otherwise, separate teams can each deliver a working component while the assembled system fails the people using it.

We will use that reasoning for an invented pump inspection service. The arithmetic can tell us whether a proposed inspection policy meets stated limits. Whether the predictions are good enough still needs evidence from representative pumps. First principles give us a way to question the design; they do not supply missing measurements.

reading.experimentTitle: How much inspection work does this policy create?
reading.experimentIntro: Change the inspection decisions or the time each inspection takes. Botie totals the work the team would receive.
reading.connectionTitle: From a prediction to an appointment
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Allocate the inspection time
reading.exampleNote: These are invented maintenance records, with one row per pump.

intuition.title: Follow one warning
intuition.explanation: A warning needs a recipient and an action before it can help a pump.

scene.caption: The model is one part of the decision procedure.

intuition.title: Count the work that reaches the team
intuition.explanation: These decisions schedule two inspections. Their durations differ, so counting warnings alone would miss the time requirement.

scene.caption: 1 means schedule an inspection; 0 means defer.

parts.title: 1. Name the action someone can take
paragraphs: “Predict failures” leaves several questions unanswered. A failure next year and a failure before tomorrow’s shift require different responses. For this service, the decision is whether to schedule an inspection during the next shift. A technician receives the assignment and records what they find.

A software example follows the same reasoning. If we predict that a support message is urgent, who will move it ahead in the queue? The prediction needs an agreed action and enough time for that action to help.
interpretation: Write the action in ordinary language before choosing the model output. If nobody can act on the answer, revisit the problem.

parts.title: 2. Separate the outcome from the signal
paragraphs: The outcome we care about is avoidable pump downtime. The model sees measurements such as vibration and temperature. An inspection finding is another observation, while a risk score is an estimate produced from observations. These are different things.

We might label a training row by whether a fault was found within a day. That label is convenient, but only inspected pumps get findings. A model trained on those records may learn the old inspection policy as well as the faults. Ask how each label becomes observable.
interpretation: A proxy is a measurable substitute for something we care about. State what it misses. More warnings is a poor substitute for less downtime.

parts.title: 3. Turn “manageable” into a limit
paragraphs: The maintenance team has 60 inspection minutes available in this small example. Each proposed assignment consumes part of that time. Represent a decision with 1 for inspect and 0 for defer. Multiplying a decision by its duration gives the minutes assigned to that pump.
The inputs are aligned lists: the first decision and first duration both belong to pump A. A dot product multiplies matching entries and adds the contributions.
parts.calculation:
Decisions = [1, 0, 1]
Durations in minutes = [20, 40, 30]
Assigned minutes = 1 × 20 + 0 × 40 + 1 × 30 = 50
Remaining minutes = 60 − 50 = 10
interpretation: The policy fits the time budget. We have not yet shown that it chooses the pumps that most need help.

examples.title: Count a different pair of appointments
paragraphs: NumPy stores the decisions and durations in one-dimensional arrays. Their positions must describe the same pumps.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
decisions = np.array([1, 1, 0])
minutes = np.array([15, 25, 35])
print(int(decisions @ minutes))
interpretation: The scalar result is total scheduled time. The zero prevents the third duration from contributing.

parts.title: 4. Keep facts separate from assumptions
paragraphs: A shift length may be a contractual limit. Inspection duration is usually an estimate with variation. The chance that an inspection prevents a breakdown is a further assumption that needs evidence. Writing all of these as bare numbers makes them look equally certain.

Keep a small design record: what each quantity means, its units, where it came from, and what range seems plausible. For an unknown duration, a timed trial tells us more than another decimal place in the estimate.
interpretation: We will deliberately vary these assumptions in later workshops. The design should make it clear which measurement could change our decision.

parts.title: 5. Give the model an information boundary
paragraphs: A prediction made before a shift can use earlier sensor readings. It cannot use the technician’s later findings. Define a prediction time and an outcome window before assembling training rows.

Also decide what happens when readings are missing. A missing temperature should not silently become a normal temperature. The design may defer to a technician, use a documented fallback, or decline to make a prediction.
interpretation: The next lessons develop this boundary into a testable data contract.

parts.title: 6. Write a requirement we can check
paragraphs: “The service should be useful” gives us no acceptance test. “The scheduled inspections must fit the available minutes” gives us an immediate calculation. Predictive usefulness needs a separate requirement, such as a limit on missed faults in a representative evaluation, with its sample size reported.

A requirement also needs an owner. Someone must decide whether a miss is tolerable and what evidence would justify changing that limit. An engineer should not quietly bury those choices inside a default threshold.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop handles the scheduling calculation. Our Python challenge also reports remaining capacity, including a negative result when the proposed schedule is too long.

quiz.prompt: What should we investigate before learning from those labels?
options: Whether the labelled pumps represent all pumps we will score
Whether every uninspected pump can be labelled healthy
Whether the pump IDs are in alphabetical order
quiz.because: Inspection affects which outcomes become visible. An absent label does not mean a healthy pump.

given.data: Only inspected pumps receive confirmed fault labels. The old team mainly inspected hot pumps.

quiz.prompt: This proves that the model finds useful inspections.
quiz.because: Capacity and predictive usefulness need different evidence.

Use decisions [1,0,1,1], durations [12,30,18,25], and available time 50. Print the returned list. Keep a negative remainder so an overbooked shift is visible.

import numpy as np

def schedule(decisions, minutes, available):
    # Validate the inputs, then calculate used and remaining time.

Multiply each duration by its 0-or-1 decision, then collect the assigned minutes with Add a list. A dot product would perform the same calculation.

title: Do We Need a Learned Model Yet?
blurb: A fixed rule already catches some faults. Work out what a learned model would have to improve before paying for its extra work.
openingTitle: The Temperature Rule Already Catches Some Problems
opening: Botie can send an inspection request whenever a pump gets unusually hot. It is a simple rule, and it will miss some faults. Before replacing it with a trained model, we should find out where it helps and where it fails.
A model might catch more faults while creating extra inspections. We need a comparison that accounts for both effects, using the same pumps and the same opportunity to act.

history.title: Learning Needs Something to Improve On

sources.title: Martin Zinkevich: Rules of Machine Learning

blocks: Google’s Rules of Machine Learning recommends starting without machine learning when the necessary data are not available, and establishing metrics early. A working heuristic can make a service useful while its team learns what the problem actually demands.

For our inspection service, the temperature rule provides that first comparison. We will assign invented costs to missed faults and inspections. Those values explain the calculation; a real maintenance team would need to justify its own costs and any limits that cannot be traded away.

reading.experimentTitle: Which policy loses less on the same pumps?
reading.experimentIntro: Change the fault labels, decisions, or costs. Compare each policy under the same assumptions.
reading.connectionTitle: Give a more complicated design a reason to exist
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Compare inspection policies fairly
reading.outputLabel: Policy loss in illustrative cost units
reading.exampleNote: This cost model is an invented comparison, not a measured financial return.

intuition.title: Keep the pumps fixed
intuition.explanation: A fair comparison gives both policies the same cases. Fault labels are known here because this is a retrospective exercise.

scene.caption: The model catches an extra fault but still sends one healthy pump for inspection.

intuition.title: Name what each outcome costs
intuition.explanation: An inspection costs time whether or not a fault is found. A missed fault adds a separate loss.

scene.caption: We assume an inspection catches the fault in this teaching example.

parts.title: 1. Start with a rule we can explain
paragraphs: A baseline is a procedure we can run before adding sophistication. It might inspect pumps above a fixed temperature or show the most frequently requested help article. It gives us an answer to compare against and often exposes missing infrastructure early.
Run that rule through the complete path from input to action. Discovering that warnings reach nobody is useful before spending a week tuning a model.
interpretation: Keep the baseline available throughout development. A candidate should earn its extra maintenance burden.

parts.title: 2. Put both policies on the same evidence
paragraphs: Use pumps from the same evaluation period, with fault outcomes obtained in a comparable way. Preserve a separate development set for choosing thresholds. Otherwise, repeatedly adjusting the model to beat the evaluation pumps turns them into training information.

The fault labels below are supplied for every pump. Real inspection data may lack that coverage. A fair trial might need some independently sampled inspections to learn about pumps the old policy ignored.
interpretation: Missing outcomes weaken the comparison. They cannot be repaired simply by giving uninspected pumps a healthy label.

parts.title: 3. Charge for the action and the miss
paragraphs: Let a decision of 1 mean inspect. Subtracting it from 1 identifies a deferred pump. Multiplying that result by the fault label identifies a missed fault. An inspection has a fixed cost in this example, even when the pump is healthy.
We assume inspection prevents the whole stated miss loss. If inspection sometimes fails to help, the outcome model needs another term.
parts.calculation:
Labels = [1, 0, 1, 0]
Rule decisions = [1, 1, 0, 0]
Misses = labels × (1 − decisions) = [0, 0, 1, 0]
Rule loss = 3 × 2 inspections + 20 × 1 miss = 26
Model decisions = [1, 0, 1, 1]
Model loss = 3 × 3 inspections + 20 × 0 misses = 9
interpretation: On these pumps and these costs, the model has lower decision loss. That statement still depends on the evidence and assumptions.

examples.title: Find the misses before costing them
paragraphs: Boolean comparisons can show which faulty pumps a policy defers. These arrays align one position per pump.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
fault = np.array([1, 0, 1])
inspect = np.array([0, 1, 1])
missed = (fault == 1) & (inspect == 0)
print(missed.tolist())
interpretation: The middle pump incurs an inspection, but it is not a missed fault.

parts.title: 4. Count the work needed to keep it running
paragraphs: Training a model once is only part of its cost. Someone must maintain input definitions, investigate failed requests, collect later labels, and check new versions. The heat rule also needs maintenance, so compare the additional burden fairly.

Use the same time horizon. A monthly operating estimate cannot be added directly to a loss measured over four pumps. First estimate how many comparable decisions occur in a month and how uncertain that extrapolation is.
interpretation: A small measured improvement may disappear under a plausible operating cost. That is a reason to gather better evidence, not automatically a reason to abandon ML.

parts.title: 5. Some requirements stay outside the cost score
paragraphs: If a requirement says the team can perform only a certain number of inspections, a low cost score does not grant extra capacity. Check the hard limit separately. The same applies to a service that must respond before a machine’s next cycle.
A weighted score allows one quantity to compensate for another. Use it only where that trade is actually acceptable. We will make this distinction explicit when comparing several designs.
interpretation: Inspect-all can be a useful reference policy, even if it is infeasible. It reveals how much of the apparent improvement comes from doing more work.

parts.title: 6. Choose the next experiment from the disagreement
paragraphs: Find the pumps where the baseline and candidate disagree. Are those cases genuinely different, or does the candidate rely on a sensor that is often unavailable? Examine which conditions create misses, then decide what additional observations would clarify them.

Report results by relevant operating condition as well as overall. A rule that works for one pump family may fail on another. Improvement on this tiny table is an arithmetic fact, not evidence of generalisation.
interpretation: Botie will calculate the loss for several policies. Python will package that calculation so we can compare new aligned records without rewriting it.

quiz.prompt: What does this estimate suggest?
options: The proposed model does not yet justify its extra cost
The model must be deployed because its prediction score improved
quiz.because: Compare the additional benefit and burden on the same horizon.

given.data: A model saves an estimated 50 units each month but adds 80 units of monthly upkeep. Other consequences are assumed equal.

quiz.prompt: It meets the capacity requirement.
quiz.because: A soft cost score cannot override a hard limit.

given.data: A policy has the lowest cost score but requires more inspections than the team can perform.

practice.question: Can the same calculation judge a new inspection policy?

For labels [1,0,1,0,1], compare decisions [1,1,0,0,0] and [1,0,1,0,0], with inspection cost 4 and miss cost 15. Print the two losses as a list.

import numpy as np

def policy_loss(labels, decisions, inspection_cost, miss_cost):
    pass

y = [1,0,1,0,1]
print([policy_loss(y, d, 4, 15) for d in [[1,1,0,0,0], [1,0,1,0,0]]])
hints: Count all inspections, including healthy pumps.
A miss needs both a fault and a decision to defer.

build.problem: Botie needs a comparison that charges for inspections and missed faults on the same pump records.
build.challenge: Construct the per-pump loss, then add it. A miss occurs when a fault label is 1 and the inspection decision is 0.
build.why: The two terms represent different consequences. Adding them makes the cost assumptions visible.
build.limitation: Fault labels are supplied for all pumps. This omits uncertain inspection effectiveness, upkeep, and limited capacity.

Subtract each decision from 1. Multiplying that result by the fault labels marks only faulty pumps we deferred.
Multiply each branch by its cost, add the contributions, and total the list. An inspection still costs something when the pump is healthy.

title: What Can the System Know at Decision Time?
blurb: A reading can describe an earlier event and still arrive too late. Design a data contract that respects both clocks.
openingTitle: The Reading Existed. Botie Still Had Not Received It.
opening: At minute 10, Botie must decide whether to inspect a pump. One sensor recorded a vibration spike at minute 8, but its network connection delayed the message until minute 12. A historical table now contains that spike. The running system could not have used it at minute 10.

This distinction also affects software. A support article may have been written yesterday but added to a search index only this afternoon. We need to design around the information the service could actually retrieve.

history.title: A Model Inherits Its Data Dependencies

sources.title: Sculley and colleagues: Hidden Technical Debt in Machine Learning Systems (2015)

blocks: Production ML systems often depend on data produced by other systems. Sculley and colleagues described how these dependencies and changes in the surrounding system create maintenance problems that model code alone does not reveal. A field can retain its name while its meaning or availability changes.

Our two-clock example makes one such dependency explicit. Event time describes the measurement; availability time describes when our service could use it. These invented timestamps are a teaching contract, not a guarantee that every database preserves the history needed to reconstruct them.

reading.experimentTitle: Which readings were available for this decision?
reading.experimentIntro: Move the decision time or delay a record. Both clocks must be at or before the decision.
reading.connectionTitle: Reconstruct the information Botie actually had
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Enforce the time boundary
reading.outputLabel: Eligibility mask, one entry per record
reading.exampleNote: Times are minutes on the same clock. Values equal to the cutoff are eligible in this example.

intuition.title: Read both timestamps
intuition.explanation: Compare each record with the decision at minute 10. An earlier event does not undo a later arrival.

scene.caption: The availability time belongs to this service, not just the sensor.

intuition.title: Preserve the boundary through the pipeline
intuition.explanation: A retrieved record still needs its meaning checked before a model consumes it.

rows.label: Select
items: Use records available by the decision time

rows.label: Predict
items: Save the input contract and model version

scene.caption: An input contract describes what each field means and when it is usable.

parts.title: 1. An event and its arrival are different facts
paragraphs: A sensor samples the world at one time and delivers the record at another. Clocks, buffering, and network interruptions can separate them. For an offline training table, the delay is easy to overlook because all the records are now present.

A decision-time reconstruction needs the timestamp when the consuming system could actually access the record. If a later repair changes a historical value, preserve the earlier version too. The final corrected table may describe a different information state.
interpretation: Document which clock each timestamp uses and how clock disagreement is handled. A precise-looking timestamp is not proof of a synchronised clock.

parts.title: 2. Describe an input with more than its name
paragraphs: A field called temperature could mean Celsius, Fahrenheit, or a moving average calculated over a window. A feature contract should state units, shape, missing-value behaviour, and the aggregation window. It should also say which entity the record describes.
For text retrieval, include when a document version entered the index and what permissions the requester had. The existence of a document somewhere does not mean this request could retrieve it.
interpretation: These are interface requirements. A fitted model cannot reliably repair a changed meaning that the pipeline does not identify.

parts.title: 3. Build the eligibility check from two comparisons
paragraphs: Start with two yes-or-no questions for each record. Did its event happen by the cutoff? Was the record available by the cutoff? Both must hold. We use inclusive comparisons, so a record available exactly at the decision time is accepted.

In the workshop, a Threshold gate reports 1 when its first input reaches its second. Connect the cutoff to the Score input and the record timestamps to Cutoff. This tests whether the decision time has reached each timestamp. Multiplying the two binary masks implements “both”.
parts.calculation:
Event times = [8, 8, 11]
Availability times = [9, 12, 11]
Decision time = 10
Event-time mask = [1, 1, 0]
Availability mask = [1, 0, 0]
Eligible = [1, 1, 0] × [1, 0, 0] = [1, 0, 0]
interpretation: The labels on the wires matter. Reversing a comparison would admit future information.

examples.title: A boolean mask keeps record identities aligned
paragraphs: Comparison produces a boolean array of the same shape. Selection uses its True positions.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
arrival = np.array([4, 9, 6])
reading = np.array([20., 99., 24.])
known = arrival <= 6
print(known.tolist())
print(reading[known].tolist())
interpretation: This program demonstrates only the arrival check. The challenge also enforces event time and a valid timestamp order.

parts.title: 4. Eligibility does not mean freshness
paragraphs: A reading from last week can pass both comparisons. That does not make it a useful description of a pump now. Add a maximum permitted age when the task requires recent evidence, and say which timestamp the age uses.
Do not confuse a freshly delivered old reading with a fresh measurement. A freshness check usually needs event time. A separate transport monitor can detect long delivery delays.
interpretation: The workshop deliberately checks eligibility alone. A complete pump service would also choose a freshness rule and a response when no acceptable reading remains.

parts.title: 5. Labels have an availability time too
paragraphs: A fault may happen after the prediction and be confirmed several days later. The outcome window tells us what we want to predict. Label availability tells us when we can train or evaluate using the confirmed result.

For a retrospective training simulation, include only labels that would have been known at that training date. A final dataset with every later confirmation can overstate how quickly the system could have adapted.
interpretation: Keep the prediction identity so a later outcome can be joined to the correct earlier decision. An outcome must never be inserted into its own input features.

parts.title: 6. Make missing information an explicit branch
paragraphs: If no eligible reading exists, the pipeline needs a response. It might request a manual check or keep using a previous reading within a defined age limit. Filling a missing value with zero quietly assigns a numerical meaning to absence.
Record the branch taken so later evaluation includes the cases where the model could not run. Reporting accuracy only on successfully served cases hides coverage failures.
interpretation: Our reusable Python function returns an eligibility mask. The caller can then decide how to select records or handle an all-False result without pretending the evidence existed.

parts.title: 7. Test the boundary itself
paragraphs: Include records just before the cutoff, exactly at it, and just after it. Include a record with an early event and a late arrival. Those cases exercise the design rule more directly than a large random table.

This lesson assumes arrival cannot precede the event on our shared clock. A violation raises an error. Real systems with uncertain clocks may need an explicit tolerance or interval model instead of silently accepting impossible ordering.
interpretation: A contract is useful when another component can test it. The challenge’s invalid-input behaviour is part of that contract.

quiz.prompt: What does the two-clock check establish?
options: It was available, but may be too old for the task
It must be a correct measurement
quiz.because: Eligibility does not establish freshness or measurement quality.

given.data: A record has event time 2, arrival time 3, and decision time 100. No maximum age is specified.

quiz.prompt: The record passes both comparisons.
quiz.because: Equality is explicitly allowed here.

given.data: Event time and arrival time both equal the decision time. The contract uses inclusive comparisons.

practice.question: Which records could a prediction have used?

For events [2,5,8,9], arrivals [3,7,8,12], and cutoff 8, print the mask as a list.

import numpy as np

def eligible(events, arrivals, cutoff):
    pass

build.challenge: Use two threshold comparisons and combine their masks. Output 1 only when both event and availability timestamps are at or before the decision time.

title: Where Does the Prediction Pipeline Run Out of Room?
blurb: A fast model can sit inside a slow service. Follow requests through preparation, inference, and storage to find the stage that limits the whole path.
openingTitle: Why Is the Queue Growing When the Model Is Fast?
opening: Botie’s image service can classify many pictures each second. Yet users are waiting. The model is only one step: each picture must first be decoded, resized, and later written to a result store. Any of those steps can hold up the rest.
We need a small model of the service before buying more hardware. How much work can each stage finish? How quickly does new work arrive? Start with quantities we can compare in the same units.

history.title: Put Numbers Against the Boxes in a Design

sources.title: Google SRE Workbook: Non-Abstract Large System Design

blocks: A diagram can connect services without showing whether any of them can handle the proposed workload. Google’s Non-Abstract Large System Design approach develops concrete resource estimates from a system’s requirements, then revises the design as those estimates expose constraints.

Our image service is a small invented example of that process. We will use ideal stage capacities first. Those estimates help choose what to measure, but contention and scheduling overhead mean a real benchmark can disagree.

reading.experimentTitle: What capacity does each stage contribute?
reading.experimentIntro: Change worker counts and per-worker rates. The smallest stage capacity limits this ideal pipeline.
reading.connectionTitle: A request has to pass through every stage
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Locate the limiting stage
reading.outputLabel: Ideal pipeline capacity, requests per second
reading.exampleNote: The model assumes independently pipelined stages and equally shareable work.

intuition.title: Trace one image
intuition.explanation: The stages can work on different images at the same time, but each image still visits them in order.

scene.caption: Concurrent stages improve throughput; they do not remove stages from an individual request.

intuition.title: Compare capacities on one scale
intuition.explanation: Multiply worker count by rate per worker before comparing the stages.

scene.caption: Storage is the limiting stage under these assumptions.

parts.title: 1. Distinguish elapsed time from completed work
paragraphs: Latency is how long one request takes from arrival to response. Throughput is how many requests finish per unit time. A pipeline can finish many requests per second while each request spends a noticeable time travelling through it.

Imagine several images at different stages. Preparation can work on the next image while inference processes the current one. That overlap explains why adding all stage durations answers a different question from finding the smallest stage capacity.
interpretation: Keep both quantities in the design. A throughput requirement alone does not protect a user from a long wait.

parts.title: 2. Turn a worker measurement into a stage estimate
paragraphs: Measure a worker using representative images and the intended model. If one worker completes six requests each second, two independent workers would ideally complete twelve. The word independent matters: workers sharing a saturated disk may not provide twice the rate.
Our arrays use one entry per stage. Multiplying aligned worker counts and rates gives a capacity for each stage, all in requests per second.
parts.calculation:
Workers = [2, 1, 2]
Per-worker rates = [6, 20, 5] requests/s
Stage capacities = [2 × 6, 1 × 20, 2 × 5] = [12, 20, 10] requests/s
interpretation: This is an estimate to test. Treat measured per-worker rates as specific to a workload and resource allocation.

examples.title: Name the stage beside its capacity
paragraphs: Keep names in a separate aligned array so a minimum remains interpretable.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
names = np.array(["prepare", "infer", "store"])
capacity = np.array([8., 15., 11.])
i = int(np.argmin(capacity))
print(names[i])
print(float(capacity[i]))
interpretation: argmin returns a position. Indexing uses that position to recover the stage name.

parts.title: 3. Find the narrowest stage
paragraphs: Every request must pass through storage, so a storage stage that completes ten requests per second prevents the whole pipeline from sustaining more than that rate. Increasing inference capacity alone does not change this bound.

The minimum rule assumes each request visits each stage once and stages can overlap. If two stages share one worker, or some requests visit an expensive stage repeatedly, describe that shared work explicitly before taking a minimum.
parts.calculation:
Ideal pipeline capacity = min(12, 20, 10) = 10 requests/s
Incoming rate = 8 requests/s
Capacity minus demand = 10 − 8 = 2 requests/s
interpretation: Positive spare capacity is useful, but it does not prove that bursts or slow images will meet a latency target.

parts.title: 4. Check units before changing the architecture
paragraphs: A rate reported per minute must be converted before comparing it with requests per second. A batch rate is not a request rate until batch size is known. A camera producing frames and a model producing crops may not even use the same unit of work.

For example, one frame can contain several candidate objects. The detection stage’s frame rate and the classifier’s crop rate need a conversion based on crops per frame. An average may hide unusually crowded frames.
interpretation: Write the unit on the wire. The arithmetic is easy to inspect once each rate refers to the same work.

parts.title: 5. Speed up the part that changes the answer
paragraphs: If storage is limiting, first investigate that stage. More storage workers, a different write pattern, or fewer unnecessary writes may help. Once it improves, preparation may become the new limit.
The same reasoning applies to physical inspection. A model can flag pumps faster than a technician can inspect them. Increasing prediction throughput will not create inspection capacity.
interpretation: Recalculate after each proposed change. The identity of the limiting stage is a property of the whole current design.

parts.title: 6. Leave room for variation and failures
paragraphs: Operating exactly at an estimated capacity leaves no room for bursts, slow requests, or a worker going away. Choose a target using workload measurements and a service requirement. There is no universal percentage that makes every design safe.
Measure both normal and degraded conditions. If a model server loses one worker, check whether the remaining capacity can keep up and how the service handles the accumulated queue.
interpretation: Botie’s next workshop follows that queue over time. Here, Python reports all stage capacities as well as the minimum so we can see why a design is limited.

quiz.prompt: What additional interpretation is needed before comparing with a request rate?
options: Convert batches into requests using batch size
quiz.because: The unit of work must match.

given.data: A worker processes 5 batches/s, each containing 8 independent requests.

quiz.prompt: The estimate alone guarantees the latency target.
quiz.because: Queueing and request variation still need testing.

given.data: A pipeline has estimated capacity above average demand. No burst or latency measurements were taken.

build.title: Find the image service bottleneck
build.problem: Botie has worker counts and measured per-worker rates for preparation, inference, and storage.
build.challenge: Calculate stage capacities and connect the smallest capacity to Result. Do not add capacities from stages every request must visit.
build.why: The limiting stage changes as the design changes. Both arrays preserve the same stage order.
build.limitation: This ideal bound omits shared-resource contention, variable request work, and queueing delays.
