title: What Happens When Requests Arrive Together?
blurb: Average demand can fit while a burst still leaves people waiting. Follow unfinished requests from one interval to the next.
openingTitle: The Service Was Quiet, Then Everyone Uploaded a Picture
opening: Botie’s image service looks comfortably fast when we average requests over a minute. Then a class uploads its pictures together. The service must either keep those requests somewhere, reject some, or make the class wait.

A queue is the unfinished work we carry forward. We can understand its behaviour without beginning with a probability distribution. Let’s follow a short sequence of arrivals and give the server a fixed amount of work it can complete each interval.

history.title: Waiting Work Can Become Another Source of Failure

sources.title: Google SRE Book: Addressing Cascading Failures

blocks: Google’s account of cascading failures describes how overload can create growing queues, consume resources, and trigger timeouts or retries that make the overload worse. Requests waiting for service are still part of the running system.

Our queue has no timeout or retry yet. That simplification lets us see the accumulation itself. The example uses discrete intervals and invented traffic; it is not a measured latency model of a production server.

reading.experimentTitle: Will the queue drain after the burst?
reading.experimentIntro: Change arrivals or completion capacity. Each interval starts with the unfinished work left by the preceding one.
reading.connectionTitle: Work cannot disappear between intervals
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Simulate the unfinished requests
reading.outputLabel: Backlog at the end of each interval
reading.exampleNote: Arrivals enter at the start of an interval, then service occurs. The initial queue is empty.

intuition.title: Carry the unfinished work forward
intuition.explanation: Unused service capacity cannot be saved for a future burst.

scene.caption: The quiet first interval does not let the second interval complete more than four requests.

intuition.title: One interval of the queue
intuition.explanation: Start with what was already waiting, then admit new work before using this interval’s service capacity.

rows.label: Keep nonnegative
items: An empty queue has zero backlog

scene.caption: Repeat using the previous result as state.

parts.title: 1. Choose what one time step means
paragraphs: Our interval could be a second or a minute, but arrivals and service capacity must use that same interval. Arrivals are counts of requests, not a rate to add directly to a count. Here, requests arrive at the start and the server works afterward.
Changing that ordering changes results near a boundary. A finer simulation might use individual arrival and completion times. The coarse model is useful because we can inspect every step.
interpretation: We start with an empty queue. If a service already has unfinished work, that initial state must be supplied.

parts.title: 2. Account for the work that remains
paragraphs: Add the previous backlog to new arrivals. The server completes at most its capacity, so subtract that capacity and clamp a negative remainder to zero. A negative queue would mean saving unused processing slots, which the server cannot do.
parts.calculation:
backlog[t] = max(0, backlog[t−1] + arrivals[t] − capacity[t])
Initial backlog = 0
Interval 1: max(0, 0 + 2 − 4) = 0
Interval 2: max(0, 0 + 7 − 4) = 3
Interval 3: max(0, 3 + 1 − 4) = 0
interpretation: The burst creates a queue that drains in the next interval. This is a recurrence: the next answer depends on the previous answer.

parts.title: 3. Store state explicitly in Python
paragraphs: A NumPy array can hold the arrivals, but each backlog depends on the preceding one. A short loop makes that dependence clear. An elementwise subtraction would incorrectly pretend each interval starts empty.
The workshop’s Queue over time component performs this recurrence and exposes the entire backlog sequence. Its inputs are aligned arrivals and capacities, so we can model a temporary worker loss too.
interpretation: A component can contain a repeated operation once we have explained and inspected that operation.

examples.title: Follow two intervals by hand in code
paragraphs: The variable waiting carries state. Each appended result records the end of an interval.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
arrivals = np.array([5, 0])
waiting = 0
trace = []
for incoming in arrivals:
    waiting = max(0, waiting + int(incoming) - 2)
    trace.append(waiting)
print(trace)
interpretation: The second interval starts with three waiting requests, even though no new request arrives.

parts.title: 4. A stable average does not remove a burst
paragraphs: When long-run arrivals exceed sustainable service, a queue generally cannot stay bounded without dropping work. A lower average gives it a chance to drain, but a large burst can still violate a waiting-time requirement. Equality leaves no spare capacity to recover from variation.
Our sequence is finite. Seeing its queue end at zero does not prove that a future traffic pattern will behave similarly. Keep the workload assumptions beside the result.
interpretation: Measure the maximum backlog and the time to drain, not only the final queue length.

parts.title: 5. Queue length is not an individual latency measurement
paragraphs: A backlog counts requests waiting or unfinished at a boundary. Latency measures time for a particular request. To calculate individual latency, we would need service order, arrival times within the interval, and request durations.

For a first-in-first-out queue with similar jobs, more work ahead usually implies a longer wait. That intuition is useful, but dividing a coarse queue count by a rate is only an estimate under stated assumptions.
interpretation: We will report backlog directly. Calling it measured p95 latency would claim evidence this simulator does not produce.

parts.title: 6. Decide what happens at a queue limit
paragraphs: Real queues need resource limits. When full, a service may reject new work with a retry policy, defer nonurgent jobs, or run a cheaper fallback. Unlimited retries can send even more requests into an already overloaded service.

For a camera inspection system, an old frame may become useless before it reaches inference. The appropriate response could be dropping stale frames while recording the coverage gap. A support request may instead need durable storage.
interpretation: Queue policy depends on the task. Our later failure lesson will make the response explicit rather than pretending every request eventually receives a useful prediction.

parts.title: 7. Compare designs using the same arrival trace
paragraphs: Replay the same burst against alternative capacities. Also include a worker outage and a quiet recovery period. These tests help separate a capacity change from a workload change.
The Python function will reject negative or fractional request counts. If jobs have unequal work sizes, replace counts with a meaningful workload measure or simulate jobs individually.
interpretation: Botie’s construction asks for the maximum unfinished work. You will need the Queue over time component and an operation that inspects its sequence.

quiz.prompt: Which statement is supported?
options: Every request met its latency target
The service can handle all future traffic
quiz.because: The final state says nothing by itself about each request’s delay.

given.data: A trace has a large backlog halfway through and zero backlog at the end.

quiz.prompt: Those retries can increase overload.
quiz.because: They add work when the service already lacks capacity.

given.data: A waiting request triggers repeated immediate retries against the same overloaded service.

practice.title: Can you replay a burst and a worker outage?
practice.question: Can you replay a burst and a worker outage?

Use arrivals [3,8,2,0] and capacities [4,4,0,6]. Print the backlog list, then its maximum.

title: Will the Model Fit on the Device?
blurb: A model file can fit while its running process runs out of memory. Account for parameters, temporary values, and the rest of the runtime.
openingTitle: The File Fits. Why Does Inference Run Out of Memory?
opening: Botie copies a model onto an inspection device. The file is smaller than the available memory, but the process fails when it receives a batch of images. Running a model needs room for more than its saved parameters.

Let’s put names on the pieces of memory before adding them. We will separate what stays fixed from what grows with the batch, then work out how many images the device can handle under a stated estimate.

history.title: Small Devices Made the Whole Inference Engine Matter
blocks: MCUNet examined neural-network inference on microcontrollers with tight memory and compute limits. Its design combined choices about the network with an inference engine suited to those limits. A useful model had to fit the way the device actually executed it.

Our budget is much simpler. We count parameter storage, an estimated peak activation cost per example, and fixed runtime memory. We are not reproducing MCUNet’s engine or claiming that this linear estimate describes every network.

reading.experimentTitle: Where does the remaining memory go?
reading.experimentIntro: Change parameter count, storage precision, batch size, or runtime estimates. A negative remainder means the proposed allocation exceeds the budget.
reading.connectionTitle: Budget for a running model
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Find the batch that fits
reading.exampleNote: Small invented byte counts keep the arithmetic readable. All quantities use bytes, not a mixture of MB and MiB.

intuition.title: Give each allocation a place
intuition.explanation: Some memory is shared by the batch; some grows as we process more examples.

scene.caption: Peak live memory matters more than the sum of every tensor ever created.

intuition.title: Compare two batch sizes
intuition.explanation: For this toy device, parameter storage uses 40 bytes, runtime uses 12, and activations use 8 per example. The limit is 100 bytes.

scene.caption: Batch six exactly fills the estimate and leaves no allowance for errors in it.

parts.title: 1. Count bytes for the saved parameters
paragraphs: A parameter is a stored value such as a weight or bias. With a fixed-width representation, multiply the number of parameters by bytes per parameter. Eight-bit values use one byte each; 32-bit values use four. Quantised formats may also store scales and other metadata.
A file can be compressed or contain additional information, so its size need not equal the in-memory parameter allocation. Ask what the runtime loads and in which format.
parts.calculation: 10 parameters × 4 bytes/parameter = 40 bytes
interpretation: This toy count is deliberately small. The same dimensional calculation applies to a larger model.

parts.title: 2. Make room for intermediate results
paragraphs: A layer creates outputs that later layers consume. Those intermediate values are called activations. Some can be released or reused; others must remain live for a skip connection or another operation. The peak depends on which values coexist.

We will use an estimated peak activation cost per example and assume it scales with batch size. Real kernels may allocate workspaces or choose different algorithms for a larger batch, so validate that assumption by measuring peak memory.
interpretation: Summing all layer outputs without considering their lifetimes can overestimate memory. Ignoring them can underestimate it.

parts.title: 3. Keep runtime memory in the budget
paragraphs: The process also needs input and output buffers, library workspaces, and runtime state. For this exercise they are a fixed allocation. That is an accounting assumption, not a claim that runtime overhead is always fixed.
Training adds other allocations, often including gradients and optimiser state. A serving estimate that omits them cannot be reused as a training-memory guarantee.
parts.calculation:
Estimated bytes = parameter_count × bytes_per_parameter
                  + batch_size × activation_bytes_per_example
                  + runtime_bytes
For batch 2: 10 × 4 + 2 × 8 + 12 = 68 bytes
Headroom = 100 − 68 = 32 bytes
interpretation: The workshop returns headroom. A negative answer is useful feedback that the proposed design does not fit this budget.

examples.title: Separate fixed memory from batch memory
paragraphs: A vector of candidate batches lets us inspect several totals without changing the fixed allocation.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
batches = np.array([1, 2, 3])
fixed_bytes = 24
activation_bytes = 6
print((fixed_bytes + batches * activation_bytes).tolist())
interpretation: Each entry is a candidate total. These are separate proposed runs, not allocations to add together.

parts.title: 4. Solve for the maximum batch under this model
paragraphs: Subtract fixed allocations from the limit. Divide the remainder by activation bytes per example, then round down because a batch contains a whole number of examples. If the fixed allocations already exceed the limit, even batch zero fails the budget.
Our function returns zero when no positive batch fits. That is a design failure to investigate, not permission to serve an empty batch as a successful request.
parts.calculation:
Available for activations = 100 − 40 − 12 = 48 bytes
Maximum batch = floor(48 / 8) = 6
interpretation: Rounding up would exceed the limit. Exact equality fits the arithmetic but leaves no reserve for an inaccurate estimate.

parts.title: 5. Changing precision changes more than storage
paragraphs: Fewer bits can reduce parameter storage and sometimes computation. The model’s numerical behaviour may also change, and some hardware needs particular formats to gain speed. Measure prediction quality and runtime after conversion.
Shrinking parameters may have little effect when activations dominate peak memory. Inspect the allocations before deciding which optimisation is worth trying.
interpretation: A smaller file is evidence about storage. It is not by itself evidence about latency or task accuracy.

parts.title: 6. Measure the intended workload
paragraphs: Use the real input sizes, batch pattern, runtime version, and device. Variable-length text or larger images can change activation requirements. A warm process may retain allocations, and peak allocation metrics may differ from total device memory use.
Record what the measurement includes and repeat it under representative conditions. Keep a reserve chosen from that evidence rather than relying on the exact boundary of an optimistic estimate.
interpretation: Botie lets you change one allocation at a time. The Python challenge calculates the maximum batch, then tests that it obeys the limit under the stated linear model.

quiz.prompt: How should a maximum whole batch be obtained?
quiz.because: The next whole example might exceed the limit.

given.data: There are 47 bytes left for activations, at 8 bytes per example.

quiz.prompt: Its accuracy and latency still need measurement.
quiz.because: Storage reduction does not establish either result.

given.data: A model is converted to a smaller parameter format. No quality or speed tests have run.

practice.question: What is the largest batch this estimate permits?

For a 250-byte limit, 73 fixed bytes, and 24 bytes per example, print the maximum batch and its estimated total as a list.

import numpy as np

def max_batch(limit, fixed, per_example):
    pass

b = max_batch(250, 73, 24)
print([b, 73 + b*24])
hints: Subtract fixed bytes before dividing.
Use floor, then prevent a negative batch count.

tests.name: Fixed memory exceeds limit

tests.name: Reject zero activation cost

build.challenge: Calculate total bytes from the supplied allocations, then subtract that total from the memory limit. Keep negative headroom visible.

build.limitation: The model assumes linear activation scaling and fixed runtime overhead. Actual peak memory and quantised-model quality need measurement.
hints: Give parameters and activations separate branches. Each needs a count multiplied by bytes per item.
Add parameter bytes, batch activation bytes, and fixed runtime bytes. All three allocations use the same unit.
Subtract the total from the memory limit. Keep a negative answer when the batch is too large.

title: Should the Prediction Happen Here or on a Server?
blurb: Sending an image away adds work before inference can begin. Compare communication and computation, then examine what happens when the connection disappears.
openingTitle: A Faster Server Still Has to Receive the Image
opening: A camera watches parts moving through an inspection station. Botie can run a small model beside the camera or send each picture to a larger server. The server computes faster, but the picture has to get there and the result has to return before the part moves on.
There is no useful answer in “the cloud is faster” by itself. Let’s describe the path in units of time, then look at the assumptions a local-versus-remote comparison leaves out.

history.title: Communication Belongs in the Design

sources.title: Satyanarayanan: The Emergence of Edge Computing (2017)

blocks: Satyanarayanan’s discussion of edge computing describes the role of computation close to data sources when latency and bandwidth make distant processing difficult. The location of computation changes how much information has to travel and how long a response takes.

Our inspection example compares a local estimate with a simplified remote path. It does not claim that local computation always wins. A larger remote model may be more useful, and many systems divide work between the device and a server.

reading.experimentTitle: Does faster inference make up for the upload?
reading.experimentIntro: Change image size, effective bandwidth, network overhead, or compute time. The result is remote time minus local time.
reading.connectionTitle: Count the journey before choosing where to compute
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Compare two inference paths
reading.exampleNote: The estimates exclude queueing and assume negligible response payload, with return delay included in fixed overhead.

intuition.title: Follow the remote route
intuition.explanation: The server cannot classify an image it has not received.

rows.label: Upload
items: Image bytes / effective bytes per second

scene.caption: For this simplified path, the times are sequential and can be added.

intuition.title: Compare a local and a remote proposal
intuition.explanation: Both proposals must be evaluated on the same inspection task. The times here are invented.

scene.caption: A faster remote model still waits for communication.

parts.title: 1. Separate the data size from the link rate
paragraphs: Image size is an amount of data. Bandwidth is an amount per unit time. Dividing bytes by bytes per second gives seconds. Network links are often advertised in bits per second, so convert units before using that number.
Use an effective rate measured for the workload, including the practical effects that reduce payload throughput. A maximum link specification may be a poor estimate of an upload during a busy shift.
parts.calculation: Upload time = 600,000 bytes / 3,000,000 bytes per second = 0.20 s
interpretation: Compression changes the payload size. If it also changes image details, evaluate whether the inspection model loses useful evidence.

parts.title: 2. Add the time between sending and acting
paragraphs: Remote response time includes upload, network overhead, server computation, and any response payload or queueing. Our first estimate treats the response payload as negligible and includes its travel delay in a fixed overhead term.

For local inference, preparation and actuation also take time. In this toy comparison, shared preparation and actuation are excluded from both alternatives, so we compare the part of the path that differs.
parts.calculation:
Remote estimate = 0.20 + 0.04 + 0.03 = 0.27 s
Local estimate = 0.12 s
Remote minus local = 0.27 − 0.12 = 0.15 s
interpretation: A positive difference means the remote path is slower under these estimates. It says nothing yet about which model is more accurate.

parts.title: 3. Find the network conditions that change the choice
paragraphs: A smaller payload or a faster effective link can make the remote path competitive. A slower connection can reverse that result. Sweep several rates instead of treating one measurement as permanent.
NumPy can calculate a time for each candidate rate. Keep the array positions aligned so each result belongs to the intended link condition.
interpretation: The comparison becomes more useful when we see where its conclusion changes.

examples.title: Inspect two network conditions
paragraphs: This separate example uses a 200-byte teaching payload and a fixed overhead of 0.1 seconds.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
rates = np.array([1000., 2000.])
seconds = 200 / rates + 0.1
print(np.round(seconds, 2).tolist())
interpretation: Doubling bandwidth reduces the upload term. The fixed overhead remains.

parts.title: 4. Check whether the two predictions solve the same task
paragraphs: A tiny local model and a large remote model may have different errors. Compare them on representative inspection images, including difficult lighting and uncommon faults. If the remote model improves quality, decide whether that improvement is usable within the response deadline.
A hybrid might run locally for routine cases and send selected cases for review. That selection rule needs its own evaluation; a confidence score does not automatically identify all difficult cases.
interpretation: Compare whole decisions under requirements. A latency-only winner may still be unsuitable.

parts.title: 5. Treat a missing connection as a real condition
paragraphs: A disconnected camera cannot receive a remote answer by waiting for an upload estimate. Decide whether the machine can pause, use a local fallback, or record the part for later inspection. The appropriate choice depends on the consequences of proceeding.
Buffering helps only if a later answer is still useful and storage is sufficient. A stale decision about a part that has already passed the station may have no operational value.
interpretation: Do not encode a network outage as zero latency. It is an unavailable path requiring another action.

parts.title: 6. Consider energy and data exposure separately
paragraphs: Sending data can consume energy, as can local computation. The balance depends on the hardware, radio, workload, and duty cycle. Measure it when battery life is a requirement rather than assuming one location is always cheaper.

Moving images off a device also changes where data are stored and who can access them. Determine whether the task needs raw images, cropped regions, or a smaller representation, and document retention and access requirements.
interpretation: The workshop compares response-time estimates. A deployment decision also needs evidence about accuracy, resource use, and the permitted data path.

quiz.prompt: What must the design specify?
options: A timely local response, pause, or other explicit failure action
An assumption that buffering always solves the problem
quiz.because: A late answer may no longer support the action.

given.data: A camera cannot connect to the server, and each result is needed before a moving part leaves the station.

quiz.prompt: The latency comparison establishes equal usefulness.
quiz.because: Task quality requires separate evidence.

given.data: Two candidate models have equal response time. Their errors were never compared.

practice.title: How does the preferred path change with the connection?
practice.question: How does the preferred path change with the connection?
task: Write remote_seconds(payload_bytes, rates, overhead, compute). Return a NumPy array, one time per effective upload rate. Rates must be a one-dimensional array of finite positive values. The other inputs are finite nonnegative scalars. Raise ValueError otherwise.

Use payload 900 bytes, rates [3000,6000], overhead 0.05 seconds, and compute 0.02 seconds. Print remote times rounded to two decimals, then a boolean list showing which are no slower than local inference at 0.25 seconds.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def remote_seconds(payload_bytes, rates, overhead, compute):
    pass

times = remote_seconds(900, [3000,6000], .05, .02)
print(np.round(times, 2).tolist())
print((times <= .25).tolist())
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def remote_seconds(payload_bytes, rates, overhead, compute):
    r = np.asarray(rates, dtype=float)
    fixed = np.asarray([payload_bytes, overhead, compute], dtype=float)
    if r.ndim != 1 or not np.isfinite(r).all() or (r <= 0).any() or not np.isfinite(fixed).all() or (fixed < 0).any():
        raise ValueError("Invalid payload, rate, or duration")
    return payload_bytes/r + overhead + compute

times = remote_seconds(900, [3000,6000], .05, .02)
print(np.round(times, 2).tolist())
print((times <= .25).tolist())
hints: Divide the scalar payload by the rate array.
Keep full precision for the comparison; round only the printed times.

tests.code: np.testing.assert_allclose(remote_seconds(100, [100,200], .2, .3), [1.5,1.0])

tests.name: Zero payload retains overhead

title: Which Designs Are Actually Acceptable?
blurb: A design can be fast, accurate, or inexpensive without meeting the job’s requirements. Remove infeasible options before comparing the choices that remain.
openingTitle: The Fastest Model Misses Too Many Faults
opening: Botie has several candidate models for the inspection camera. One responds quickly but misses more faults. Another catches more faults but cannot respond before the part leaves the station. Which should we use?

We first need to separate requirements from preferences. A response deadline is a limit the design must meet. Among designs that meet it, we might prefer a lower operating cost. Mixing those two decisions into one score can hide an unacceptable compromise.

history.title: A Trade Study Needs Criteria Before a Winner

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: Decision Analysis

blocks: NASA’s discussion of decision analysis describes evaluating alternatives against criteria, documenting assumptions, and examining uncertainty in the comparison. A list of candidate designs does not choose its own priorities; those priorities must come from the problem being solved.

We will use a small table of invented ML evaluation results. Hard limits determine which rows are feasible. Among the remaining rows, we will identify choices that are worse on every reported objective before asking a person to make a trade-off.

reading.experimentTitle: Which candidates survive both limits?
reading.experimentIntro: Change the latency or miss limits and inspect which candidate rows remain eligible.
reading.connectionTitle: Make the unacceptable choices visible first
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Find feasible and undominated options
reading.exampleNote: Miss counts come from the same invented set of 100 faulty parts. Latency values represent the same stated benchmark statistic.

intuition.title: Keep each candidate on one row
intuition.explanation: The limits are at most 100 ms latency and at most 4 misses on the shared evaluation.

scene.caption: An excellent result in one column cannot compensate for breaking a hard limit.

intuition.title: Look for an unnecessary compromise
intuition.explanation: Among these feasible options, B is no worse than E on either quantity and better on both.

scene.caption: B and D trade speed against misses. E is dominated on these reported quantities.

parts.title: 1. Write the requirement before looking at the leaderboard
paragraphs: Suppose the part leaves the camera station after a fixed time. That gives a response deadline. The team also chooses an acceptable miss limit for the evaluation. These requirements should be justified from the task, not adjusted merely so a favourite model passes.

Specify the metric itself. Mean latency and a high latency percentile answer different questions. A miss count needs an evaluation size and population. Without those definitions, a threshold can appear precise while comparing unlike evidence.
interpretation: Our table uses the same benchmark statistic and the same 100 faulty parts for every candidate. That makes this small comparison interpretable.

parts.title: 2. Turn each requirement into a mask
paragraphs: For each candidate, compare latency with its maximum and misses with their maximum. A boolean mask records the candidates that pass one requirement. Combining the masks with AND keeps candidates that pass both.
In the workshop, use the limits as the first inputs of Threshold gates. Each gate returns 1 when its limit is at least the measured value. Multiply the resulting masks to require both conditions.
parts.calculation:
Latency = [60, 90, 120, 80] ms
Misses = [5, 3, 1, 4]
Latency at most 100: [1, 1, 0, 1]
Misses at most 4: [0, 1, 1, 1]
Feasible: [0, 1, 0, 1]
interpretation: B and D remain. Returning a mask keeps their positions aligned with the candidate names.

examples.title: Select rows without losing their names
paragraphs: A boolean mask can index the same positions in a name array and a measurement table.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
names = np.array(["small", "medium", "large"])
latency = np.array([40., 70., 130.])
print(names[latency <= 80].tolist())
interpretation: This demonstrates a single limit. The challenge needs every limit to hold for each row.

parts.title: 3. What if no candidate passes?
paragraphs: An empty feasible set is useful information. We may need to improve the implementation, collect better training data, change the operating process, or negotiate a requirement with the person responsible for it.
Do not quietly return the least bad candidate as if it passed. If a limit is a preference rather than an absolute requirement, label it that way and show the consequence of relaxing it.
interpretation: A design review should be able to say “none of these yet”. That is more useful than a ranking that hides a failed requirement.

parts.title: 4. Remove choices that lose on every reported objective
paragraphs: Among feasible candidates, say B dominates E if B is no worse on every objective and strictly better on at least one. Here, smaller latency and fewer misses are both preferred. A dominated candidate offers no improvement on either reported quantity.

Candidates that are not dominated form a Pareto set. B and D both remain because one is faster while the other misses fewer faults. This identifies the trade; it does not decide how much a miss is worth.
parts.calculation:
B = [90 ms, 3 misses]
E = [95 ms, 4 misses]
B is no worse in both columns and better in at least one
D = [80 ms, 4 misses]
D is faster than B; B misses fewer than D
Neither B nor D dominates the other
interpretation: Equal rows do not strictly dominate each other. A duplicate may still differ in an unreported property such as maintainability.

parts.title: 5. Do not add incompatible units without a reason
paragraphs: Adding milliseconds to a miss count does not produce a naturally meaningful measure. A weighted score needs a stated preference model, including scales and the meaning of each weight. Changing units can change an unjustified score’s ranking.

An explicit consequence model, such as the inspection costs from the earlier lesson, gives a more interpretable comparison when the costs are defensible. Some consequences should remain hard limits instead.
interpretation: A Pareto comparison can remove clearly inferior choices without inventing a conversion between units.

parts.title: 6. Remember that the table contains estimates
paragraphs: Latency varies, and a sample miss count does not reveal the exact future failure rate. Two close candidates may exchange places on another representative sample. Report uncertainty and relevant subgroups before treating small differences as settled.
Also check whether an omitted property changes the choice. Memory, a disconnected camera, or a requirement to explain decisions can make an apparently dominated model worth keeping.
interpretation: Dominance is relative to the objectives and evidence we supplied. Python will calculate it exactly for a table, while we remain responsible for choosing the right table.

parts.title: 7. Make the selection reproducible
paragraphs: Save the candidate versions, benchmark procedure, requirements, and reasons for the choice. If the deadline changes, someone should be able to repeat the comparison rather than infer your preferences from a final model filename.

Start with feasibility, then examine the remaining compromises. Botie’s workshop builds the first step. The second Python challenge implements dominance on a small matrix so the comparison stays inspectable.
interpretation: The functions deliberately keep all candidate positions. They return masks instead of silently renaming or reordering the designs.

quiz.prompt: Which candidate is dominated by B?
quiz.because: B is no worse than E in both columns. D is faster than B, so neither dominates the other.

given.data: Both objectives are minimised. B=[90,3], D=[80,4], E=[95,4].

quiz.prompt: One strictly dominates the other.
quiz.because: Equality gives no strict improvement.

given.data: Two candidates have identical values on every reported objective. Strict improvement in at least one objective is required for dominance.

practice.question: Can you identify the trade-offs without adding unlike units?
task: Write pareto(values) for a finite, nonempty two-dimensional table. Every column is minimised. Return a boolean array marking rows that no other row dominates. A row dominates another only if it is no worse in every column and strictly better in at least one. Invalid inputs raise ValueError.
Use [[5,5],[4,6],[6,6],[5,5],[7,3]]. Print the mask. Keep equal rows.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def pareto(values):
    pass

print(pareto([[5,5],[4,6],[6,6],[5,5],[7,3]]).tolist())
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def pareto(values):
    v = np.asarray(values, dtype=float)
    if v.ndim != 2 or not v.size or not np.isfinite(v).all():
        raise ValueError("Use a finite nonempty table")
    keep = np.ones(len(v), dtype=bool)
    for i, row in enumerate(v):
        dominates = (v <= row).all(axis=1) & (v < row).any(axis=1)
        keep[i] = not dominates.any()
    return keep

print(pareto([[5,5],[4,6],[6,6],[5,5],[7,3]]).tolist())
hints: Compare every row with the candidate being examined.
Combine no-worse-in-all with strictly-better-in-any. The candidate cannot dominate itself.

tests.name: Three-way trade
tests.code: np.testing.assert_array_equal(pareto([[1,4,4],[4,1,4],[4,4,1]]), [True,True,True])

title: Which Assumption Could Change Our Decision?
blurb: An estimate can look convincing because its uncertain inputs were hidden. Vary the assumptions and find where the preferred design changes.
openingTitle: The New Model Wins, Unless Our Cost Estimate Is Wrong
opening: Botie’s candidate catches more faults than the old rule, but it requires more inspections. Our first calculation says it is worthwhile. That conclusion depends on how costly a missed fault is, and the team only has a rough estimate.

We can inspect that dependence directly. Keep the observed policy differences fixed, vary the uncertain cost, and find where the decision changes. Then we know which missing evidence deserves attention.

history.title: Measurements Need an Account of Their Uncertainty

sources.title: NIST/SEMATECH: Uncertainty Budgets and Sensitivity Coefficients

blocks: Metrology deals with results calculated from measurements that are themselves uncertain. NIST’s handbook describes uncertainty budgets and sensitivity coefficients for tracking how inputs affect a result. Reporting only the final number can conceal which measurement contributes most to its uncertainty.

We will borrow the question about sensitivity, using a simple design comparison. Our scenarios are chosen alternatives for an uncertain cost. They are not a confidence interval, and we will not assign probabilities to them without evidence.

reading.experimentTitle: Where does the candidate stop paying for itself?
reading.experimentIntro: Change the cost per miss or the extra inspections. Positive savings favour the candidate under this cost model.
reading.connectionTitle: Show what the conclusion depends on
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Sweep an uncertain cost
reading.outputLabel: Net savings for each miss-cost scenario
reading.exampleNote: Costs and policy differences are invented. The scenario list is not a probability distribution.

intuition.title: Hold the observed difference fixed
intuition.explanation: Compared with the baseline, the candidate misses two fewer faults but requires five extra inspections. Each inspection costs 4 units.

scene.caption: The preferred policy changes with the assumed consequence of a miss.

intuition.title: Ask what we need to learn
intuition.explanation: Some inputs come from the evaluation; others still need investigation.

records.label: Extra inspections
cells: Replay the policy on later shifts

scene.caption: A sensitivity calculation helps prioritise evidence. It does not create it.

parts.title: 1. Write the difference between designs
paragraphs: We already know how to calculate a policy’s loss. Subtract candidate loss from baseline loss to obtain savings. We can simplify that difference into avoided miss loss minus added inspection cost.
This arrangement shows exactly which assumption drives the recommendation. Keep the sign convention beside it: positive savings favour the candidate, negative savings favour the baseline.
parts.calculation:
Savings = avoided_misses × cost_per_miss
          − extra_inspections × cost_per_inspection
At miss cost 20: 2 × 20 − 5 × 4 = 20 units
interpretation: The comparison covers these consequences only. Added upkeep would reduce savings further.

parts.title: 2. Try values that could plausibly change the answer
paragraphs: Use a low, central, and high estimate only if those labels mean something in the problem. You might have several documented operating scenarios instead. There is no requirement to use three.
Here we try miss costs of 5, 10, and 20 units because they show a change of sign. The list is an exploratory choice. It has no implied probability or confidence level.
interpretation: A result that stays positive across a justified range is more robust to that input than one that changes sign after a small revision.

parts.title: 3. Find the break-even value
paragraphs: At break-even, savings are zero. If avoided misses is positive, divide the extra inspection cost by the avoided miss count to find the miss cost at that boundary.

If avoided misses is zero, that division is undefined. A candidate that adds inspection work while avoiding no misses cannot justify itself through this particular benefit. A different benefit would need to be stated.
parts.calculation:
0 = 2 × cost_per_miss − 5 × 4
Break-even cost_per_miss = (5 × 4) / 2 = 10 units
interpretation: At exactly the boundary, these terms tie. A tie does not establish that the designs are equivalent in every other respect.

examples.title: A vector makes the sweep visible
paragraphs: Each input cost produces its own savings estimate. We round only for display if needed.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
miss_cost = np.array([4., 8., 12., 16.])
savings = 3*miss_cost - 6*5
print(savings.tolist())
interpretation: The sign changes within this range. The later challenge uses a different policy difference.

parts.title: 4. Sensitivity describes change, not plausibility
paragraphs: For this linear comparison, one extra unit of miss cost changes savings by the number of avoided misses. That slope is a sensitivity. It tells us how strongly the output responds, but not how likely a large cost change is.

An input with a small sensitivity can still matter if its uncertainty range is large. Conversely, a sensitive input that is measured precisely may contribute little uncertainty. Examine both properties.
interpretation: Do not call an arbitrary parameter sweep a statistical confidence interval. A probability statement needs an uncertainty model and supporting assumptions.

parts.title: 5. Change related inputs together when needed
paragraphs: The number of faults, inspection duration, and server load may all increase during the same difficult operating conditions. Varying one input at a time can miss that combination. Describe scenarios that preserve plausible relationships.

For example, a busy shift might contain more pumps and longer inspections because access is harder. A design that passes isolated changes could fail their combination. On the other hand, combining every worst value may describe an impossible scenario.
interpretation: Keep a reason for each scenario and identify which conditions the design promises to handle.

parts.title: 6. Choose the next measurement deliberately
paragraphs: If the recommendation changes within a plausible miss-cost range, review the evidence for that cost before polishing a model score. If capacity fails under the busy-shift scenario, measure inspection duration there.

There may also be a reason to choose a design that is slightly worse under the central estimate but acceptable across more plausible conditions. Explain the trade to the person responsible for the decision.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop leaves the uncertain inputs connected to the calculation. The conclusion can move when the assumptions move.

quiz.prompt: What should we call the results?
quiz.because: The chosen scenarios have no statistical coverage claim.

given.data: Costs [5,10,20] were chosen to explore outcomes. No distribution was fitted.

quiz.prompt: Testing those changes together may reveal a failure that isolated sweeps miss.
quiz.because: Related inputs can interact through capacity and waiting time.

given.data: Busy shifts increase both request volume and job duration.

practice.title: Under which cost assumptions does the candidate help?
practice.question: Under which cost assumptions does the candidate help?
task: Write savings(avoided, extra, inspection_cost, miss_costs). Return a NumPy array of net savings. avoided, extra, and inspection_cost are finite nonnegative scalars; miss_costs is a one-dimensional finite nonnegative array. Raise ValueError for invalid inputs.
Use 3 avoided misses, 8 extra inspections costing 6 each, and miss costs [10,16,25]. Print the savings list, then a list showing strictly positive savings.
practice.starter:
import numpy as np

def savings(avoided, extra, inspection_cost, miss_costs):
    pass

net = savings(3, 8, 6, [10,16,25])
print(net.tolist())
print((net > 0).tolist())
practice.solution:
import numpy as np

def savings(avoided, extra, inspection_cost, miss_costs):
    costs = np.asarray(miss_costs, dtype=float)
    fixed = np.asarray([avoided, extra, inspection_cost], dtype=float)
    if costs.ndim != 1 or not np.isfinite(costs).all() or (costs < 0).any() or not np.isfinite(fixed).all() or (fixed < 0).any():
        raise ValueError("Use finite nonnegative assumptions")
    return avoided*costs - extra*inspection_cost

net = savings(3, 8, 6, [10,16,25])
print(net.tolist())
print((net > 0).tolist())
hints: Compute the extra inspection cost once.
A zero result ties on these costs; use > rather than >= for strictly positive.

tests.name: No avoided misses
tests.code: np.testing.assert_allclose(savings(0, 2, 3, [1,100]), [-6,-6])

tests.name: No extra inspections
tests.code: np.testing.assert_allclose(savings(2, 0, 4, [0,3]), [0,6])

tests.name: Reject negative scenario cost

build.why: One input remains a list of scenarios, so the calculation returns one conclusion per assumption instead of hiding the range.
build.limitation: These are conditional estimates, not confidence bounds. Policy effects, upkeep, and relationships between uncertain inputs need separate evidence.

Multiply avoided misses by the list of miss-cost scenarios, then subtract extra inspections times inspection cost. Leave the result as a list so we can compare assumptions.

title: What Should the Prototype Teach Us?
blurb: A prototype should answer a question that could change the design. Test interacting choices together instead of changing everything and guessing what helped.
openingTitle: Batching Helped Yesterday. Why Is It Slower Today?
opening: Botie tries a larger batch and a smaller numerical format to make inference cheaper. The combined result looks promising. But how much came from each change, and would the smaller format help at the original batch size?
We can answer that with a small planned comparison. Run every combination of the two choices, keep the workload comparable, and inspect whether one change alters the effect of the other.

history.title: One Change at a Time Can Miss an Interaction
blocks: Experimental design gives engineers ways to learn from planned changes to a process. NIST’s handbook describes factorial designs, which include combinations of factor levels. Those combinations let us investigate whether the effect of one factor depends on another.

Our prototype varies batch size and parameter format. We will calculate a difference of differences in illustrative timing measurements. This is a descriptive contrast, not a complete statistical experiment or a fitted significance test.

reading.experimentTitle: Does the format change help equally at both batch sizes?
reading.experimentIntro: Enter the four batch-duration measurements in the stated order. Compare the format change at the large batch with its effect at the small batch.
reading.connectionTitle: Use a prototype to separate competing explanations
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Measure the interaction
reading.exampleNote: Timings are invented total batch durations, not per-request latency measurements.

intuition.title: Run every combination
intuition.explanation: The rows are batch sizes and the columns are formats. All measurements use the same device and image shape.

scene.caption: The format change reduces total batch time by different amounts.

intuition.title: Compare changes, not just final numbers
intuition.explanation: Subtract original-format time from smaller-format time within each row.

scene.caption: The interaction contrast compares these effects. Negative means a larger time reduction at the large batch.

parts.title: 1. Ask a question whose answer would change the plan
paragraphs: “Try optimisation” is too vague to judge a prototype. A useful question here is whether the smaller format reduces batch duration enough to justify its conversion work, and whether that depends on batch size.
State what would count as useful evidence before running the trial. If prediction quality falls below a required limit, a faster run will not rescue that candidate.
interpretation: A prototype can reject an idea cheaply. It need not become the final service to be valuable.

parts.title: 2. Name the factors and the response
paragraphs: A factor is something we deliberately vary. Our factors are batch size and parameter format, each with two chosen levels. The response is total time to process a batch. Keep the device, runtime version, and image dimensions controlled or recorded.

A large batch contains more images, so total duration alone does not establish per-image throughput or interactive latency. Calculate the relevant additional metric before choosing a deployment setting.
interpretation: The four-cell table keeps each timing attached to the choices that produced it.

parts.title: 3. Calculate each format effect at a fixed batch size
paragraphs: Within the small batch, subtract original-format duration from smaller-format duration. Repeat for the large batch. Holding batch size fixed within each subtraction avoids attributing the extra work of a larger batch to format alone.
parts.calculation:
Small-batch format effect = 30 − 40 = −10 ms
Large-batch format effect = 40 − 80 = −40 ms
interpretation: A negative effect means a shorter batch duration. The unequal changes suggest that the choices interact in these measurements.

parts.title: 4. Subtract the two effects
paragraphs: Our interaction contrast is the large-batch format effect minus the small-batch format effect. A zero contrast means equal absolute format effects at these selected batch sizes. It does not establish equal percentage changes.
Different statistical models scale interaction coefficients differently. We report this raw difference of differences, with its units and sign convention, so there is no hidden factor in the result.
parts.calculation: Interaction contrast = (40 − 80) − (30 − 40) = −30 ms
interpretation: The format reduction is associated with a larger absolute time saving at the large batch in this table.

examples.title: Read a factorial table by row
paragraphs: Rows represent small then large batches; columns represent original then smaller formats.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
times = np.array([[20., 18.], [50., 40.]])
format_effect = times[:, 1] - times[:, 0]
print(format_effect.tolist())
interpretation: The colon selects both rows. Column subtraction compares formats at the same batch size. The challenge adds the interaction contrast.

parts.title: 5. Repeat and vary the execution order
paragraphs: A single timing can reflect background work, warming, or thermal behaviour. Repeat each condition and vary the order so a gradual slowdown does not always affect the same candidate. Keep warm-up and measurement procedures consistent.
When operating conditions differ in a known way, compare within blocks such as devices or sessions. Preserve the individual measurements so we can inspect spread rather than only a rounded mean.
interpretation: Repeated measurements support uncertainty estimates. Four isolated numbers cannot by themselves establish statistical significance.

parts.title: 6. Measure whether the prediction still does its job
paragraphs: Numerical changes can alter outputs. Evaluate the converted model on the same representative labelled cases and inspect important disagreements. Changing batching should also preserve the intended relationship between each input and output.
Keep preprocessing and evaluation mode consistent. A timing benchmark that accidentally enables a training-dependent layer may compare different behaviours as well as different speeds.
interpretation: The prototype should return both operational evidence and task-quality evidence. They answer different design questions.

parts.title: 7. Decide what to try next from the pattern
paragraphs: If the format change helps only at larger batches, investigate the runtime’s execution choices and whether real traffic can fill those batches in time. A service with sparse arrivals may spend its savings waiting to form a batch.
A physical inspection station might instead have a predictable frame stream. The same benchmark can lead to different designs because the work arrives differently.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop calculates the contrast. The conclusion remains conditional on this workload, these factor levels, and the measurement procedure.

quiz.prompt: Which design change helps separate candidate effects from run order?
options: Vary the order and repeat each condition
Keep one measurement from each condition
Always make the faster-looking candidate run first
quiz.because: Execution order can otherwise be confounded with the candidate.

given.data: A benchmark always runs candidate B last, and the device gradually heats up.

quiz.prompt: The timing result alone establishes an acceptable replacement.
quiz.because: Task quality and other requirements still need evidence.

given.data: A smaller numerical format reduces batch duration. Quality has not been evaluated.

title: What Should Happen When the Model Cannot Help?
blurb: A missing reading or unavailable model still requires a response. Build a route that makes the failure visible and sends the case somewhere useful.
openingTitle: Botie Lost the Reading. The Pump Did Not Stop Existing.
opening: The inspection service expects a recent sensor record. Today the network delivers an old one, and one pump has no valid record at all. The system still has to decide what to do with those pumps.

We should decide that behaviour before a failure occurs. We will build a routing rule that uses model output only when its input checks pass and otherwise requests a separate review. Then we will examine what that fallback itself requires.

history.title: A Busy Service Needs a Defined Reduced Behaviour
blocks: Google’s discussion of overload describes controlling work when a service cannot fulfil every request normally. Admission decisions and degraded responses can prevent excess work from overwhelming the remaining capacity. The useful behaviour depends on which work the service can safely defer or simplify.

For our inspection example, an unusable sensor record routes to review. That is an illustrative policy chosen for this lesson. A real inspection process would need to establish who reviews the case, how soon, and what happens if that route is also unavailable.

reading.experimentTitle: Which pumps need the fallback route?
reading.experimentIntro: Change record validity and age. A valid record at or below the maximum age uses the model decision; otherwise it receives the review code.
reading.connectionTitle: A failed precondition needs a visible response
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Route unusable inputs
reading.exampleNote: Review is a separate operational route. It is not an automatic guarantee that a fault will be found.

intuition.title: Check the evidence before using the decision
intuition.explanation: The maximum age is five minutes. Model decisions use 0 for defer and 1 for inspect.

scene.caption: A plausible model output cannot repair an invalid or stale input.

intuition.title: Keep the fallback in the same decision path
intuition.explanation: Both branches must produce an action the next component understands.

rows.label: Otherwise
items: Route to review and record the reason

scene.caption: Do not count routed-away cases as successful model predictions.

parts.title: 1. List the conditions the model depends on
paragraphs: Start with the assumptions we already identified: the record belongs to the right pump, its units match, and its timestamp is usable. Add runtime availability and any other condition required for a prediction.

For this workshop, a supplied validity flag summarises the schema checks. Record age is checked separately. That division lets us see what the routing rule does without hiding every input check inside one component.
interpretation: A validity flag is an observed precondition result. It is not the model’s confidence in its own prediction.

parts.title: 2. Choose a meaning for every outcome
paragraphs: Our model proposes either defer or inspect. An unusable input gets a third code, review, so downstream code can distinguish it from an ordinary defer decision. The number −1 is just an identifier for that route.
A review task needs enough context to be useful, including the pump identity and why the automated path declined. Do not display a normal-looking answer while silently using a different procedure.
interpretation: Fallback behaviour should be visible in logs and evaluation as well as in the user-facing process.

parts.title: 3. Build the use-model mask
paragraphs: First compare the maximum age with every record age. Then require both that freshness check and the supplied validity flag. These binary values combine with multiplication in the workshop.
Choose by a mask then takes the model’s value at each 1 and the fallback value at each 0. It preserves pump order and does not average the two routes.
parts.calculation:
Valid = [1, 1, 0]
Ages = [2, 9, 1] minutes
Maximum age = 5 minutes
Fresh = [1, 0, 1]
Use model = valid × fresh = [1, 0, 0]
Model actions = [1, 0, 1]
Review actions = [−1, −1, −1]
Chosen actions = [1, −1, −1]
interpretation: The third pump’s fresh-looking timestamp does not override its invalid record.

examples.title: Select a route without changing the order
paragraphs: np.where chooses between aligned values using a boolean mask. It does not validate the mask’s meaning for us.
examples.code:
import numpy as np
use_model = np.array([True, False])
model_action = np.array([0, 1])
chosen = np.where(use_model, model_action, -1)
print(chosen.tolist())
interpretation: The first pump keeps its defer decision. The second is routed to review, regardless of its proposed model action.

parts.title: 4. Do not mistake confidence for a health check
paragraphs: A model can produce a high score from malformed or unfamiliar inputs. A confidence threshold may be useful for a carefully evaluated abstention policy, but it does not replace schema or freshness checks.
If confidence determines whether to answer, evaluate both error on answered cases and the fraction of cases answered. Otherwise, a system can appear accurate by declining nearly everything.
interpretation: Our route uses explicit preconditions. Adding a confidence-based route would require another contract and evaluation.

parts.title: 5. Budget the fallback too
paragraphs: Manual review has capacity and delay, just like inference. A sensor outage affecting every pump can overwhelm a review queue that usually receives only a few cases. Test that scenario.

If the normal path and fallback depend on the same unavailable server, the apparent backup may fail at the same time. Draw those dependencies and choose a response that still exists under the failure being handled.
interpretation: A fallback is part of the design, with its own limits. It is not a word that makes a failure disappear.

parts.title: 6. Decide how the system recovers
paragraphs: When readings return, check that they are fresh and valid before restoring the normal route. Keep the compatible model and preprocessing versions together. A retry should have a limit and should not amplify an outage with endless immediate work.
Preserve records of which route each case took. Later outcomes can then reveal whether the fallback met its purpose and whether a recurring input failure needs a repair upstream.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop tests routing. A real recovery test also exercises ownership, capacity, timing, and the transition back to normal service.

quiz.prompt: What does the design need to check?
options: Whether review capacity and response time can handle the outage
Only whether the model returns finite numbers
Whether the fallback has a reassuring name
quiz.because: The fallback can itself become overloaded.

given.data: A sensor outage routes every pump to a manual queue normally handling only a few cases.

quiz.prompt: Confidence proves that the input contract passed.
quiz.because: Input validity and prediction confidence are different checks.

given.data: A model returns high confidence for a malformed input.

build.why: The mask enforces preconditions before choosing the action. The review code remains distinguishable from an ordinary prediction.
build.limitation: The review team needs its own capacity and response policy. This routing calculation does not prove that manual review is effective or timely.

title: Can We Defend the Inspection Service Design?
blurb: Bring the requirements back to the complete service. Check fault misses and queue capacity separately, then identify what the prototype still has not demonstrated.
openingTitle: Botie Is Ready for a Trial. What Evidence Is Still Missing?
opening: We began with a team that needed useful pump inspections. Now we have a model proposal, resource estimates, and a fallback route. Before calling the design ready, let’s return to the original decision and check what our evidence actually establishes.

A model can catch the required faults while its queue overflows. A service can stay responsive while missing too many faults. Our review will keep those failures separate and then ask which other claims still need a real trial.

history.title: Meeting a Specification and Solving the Problem Need Different Checks

sources.title: NASA Systems Engineering Handbook: Product Realization

blocks: NASA’s product-realisation guidance distinguishes verification against specified requirements from validation against intended use and stakeholder expectations. Both matter: a system can satisfy a written specification that does not adequately describe the real need.

Our capstone verifies two numerical requirements on invented inspection and workload fixtures. It then asks what evidence would validate the service for the maintenance team. Passing the arithmetic is useful, but it cannot demonstrate fewer real breakdowns or an acceptable review workload.

reading.experimentTitle: Does this candidate pass both checks?
reading.experimentIntro: Change the decisions or workload trace. The design passes this toy review only when both the miss limit and maximum backlog limit hold.
reading.connectionTitle: Trace each claim back to its evidence
reading.practiceTitle: Practice. Write the design review report
reading.outputLabel: Review result: 1 = both numerical checks pass
reading.exampleNote: Fault records and request-arrival traces are separate fixtures. Their array lengths do not need to match.

intuition.title: Put the requirement beside its test
intuition.explanation: The first check needs known fault outcomes. The second needs a workload trace and a service model.

records.label: At most 1 missed fault
cells: Aligned fault labels and inspection decisions

records.label: Backlog never above 3 requests
cells: Arrivals and completion capacities per interval

scene.caption: A pass needs both checks. Neither is a substitute for the other.

intuition.title: Compare two failure modes
intuition.explanation: These are outcomes from separate invented review cases.

scene.caption: A single total score would make the reason for failure harder to see.

parts.title: 1. Restate the promise in terms of the maintenance team
paragraphs: The service should help schedule timely inspections within available resources. Its model score is evidence about one part of that promise. The inspection team’s capacity, the usefulness of a warning, and the time available to act all remain relevant.

For a software support service, the same review asks whether useful answers or routing decisions arrive in time and whether unresolved cases reach a workable fallback. Start with the person’s decision in both settings.
interpretation: A design review returns to the original need so it does not become a celebration of an impressive component.

parts.title: 2. Attach a test to each numerical requirement
paragraphs: For this capstone, we require at most one missed fault on the stated evaluation fixture and a maximum backlog of three requests on the stated arrival trace. These are toy acceptance criteria, not universal limits.

The quality test and load test use different data. Fault labels align with inspection decisions. Arrivals align with service capacities. There is no reason for the two pairs to have the same number of entries.
interpretation: A test specification needs units, timing conventions, and boundary behaviour. Both limits here are inclusive.

parts.title: 3. Calculate the misses from decisions and outcomes
paragraphs: The model proposes inspection decisions, and the fixture supplies confirmed faults. A fault that was deferred contributes one miss. Count those cases without confusing them with inspections of healthy pumps.
parts.calculation:
Fault labels = [1, 0, 1, 1]
Inspect decisions = [1, 0, 0, 1]
Miss indicators = labels × (1 − decisions) = [0, 0, 1, 0]
Missed faults = 1
Miss limit = 1: passes
interpretation: False alarms still matter to the wider design, but this particular requirement concerns misses. Add their inspection burden to a separate capacity check when reviewing a real policy.

parts.title: 4. Replay the workload instead of looking only at its average
paragraphs: Use the queue recurrence from the earlier lesson. Requests arrive before service in each interval, and the queue starts empty. Inspect the maximum backlog across the whole trace.
A final backlog of zero can hide an earlier overflow. The service must have enough room at every point covered by this model.
parts.calculation:
Arrivals = [2, 7, 1]
Service capacities = [4, 4, 4]
End backlogs = [0, 3, 0]
Peak backlog = 3
Backlog limit = 3: passes
interpretation: This is a queue-capacity check. It does not certify a request-latency percentile.

parts.title: 5. Report each check before the overall decision
paragraphs: An overall boolean is convenient for automation, but a person needs the measured values and failed requirements. Return a small report with missed faults, peak backlog, and whether both pass.
Keep an all-pass decision strict: one failed hard requirement means this review does not pass. Do not average the flags or let one excellent metric compensate for another.
interpretation: A Python dictionary gives the outputs names. That makes later review clearer than a list of unexplained numbers.

examples.title: Give review results meaningful names
paragraphs: This example assembles a report from already calculated values. The challenge must calculate those values from the underlying fixtures.
examples.code:
missed = 2
peak = 1
report = {"missed_faults": missed, "peak_backlog": peak, "passed": missed <= 1 and peak <= 3}
print(report)
interpretation: The dictionary keys explain the values. The overall result is False because the miss requirement fails.

parts.title: 6. Distinguish a verified calculation from a validated service
paragraphs: Passing these fixtures verifies the stated calculations and acceptance rule. It does not establish that the evaluation represents tomorrow’s pumps, that inspections actually prevent failures, or that a human can use the interface without confusion.

Validation needs evidence from intended use. A limited trial can reveal whether warnings are understandable and timely, whether the review route is overloaded, and which conditions the dataset missed. Define the trial’s limits and observation plan before using it to make broader claims.
interpretation: A successful unit test, a representative model evaluation, and an operational trial answer different questions. Record which claim each one supports.

parts.title: 7. Test the ways the design could fail
paragraphs: Change one part deliberately: miss another fault, add a burst, remove service capacity, or make a sensor record stale. The relevant check should detect the change. If everything still passes, inspect whether the test is observing the right output.

Also test valid boundaries and recovery. A service that rejects malformed records but cannot resume when valid data returns is still incomplete. Keep failures understandable so Botie can point to the component that needs attention.
interpretation: The workshop fixtures include a quality failure and an overload failure. The Python tests also use new values so a memorised answer cannot satisfy the review.

parts.title: 8. Leave a record someone else can question
paragraphs: Record the chosen design, assumptions, alternatives, and evidence behind the decision. Preserve model and data versions, and identify the conditions that would trigger another review. A new camera or changed workload can invalidate an old estimate without changing the model code.

End with unresolved questions where they remain. If the model only wins under an uncertain miss-cost estimate, state that dependence and the measurement needed next. A useful design review makes those uncertainties easier to investigate.
interpretation: Botie’s workshop combines the operations you have already built. The challenge is to connect them to the correct evidence and explain what a passing result does and does not mean.

quiz.prompt: Which conclusion is supported?
options: The service has proven that it reduces real downtime
quiz.because: Verification against fixtures has a limited scope. Intended-use claims need further evidence.

given.data: A candidate passes both numerical fixtures. No maintenance team has used it and no representative field trial has run.

quiz.prompt: The different lengths are acceptable.
quiz.because: They are separate tests of different properties, not rows to join by position.

given.data: The fault fixture has four pumps and the load fixture has three intervals. Each fixture is internally aligned.

quiz.prompt: What should happen to the old conclusion?
options: Revisit the assumptions and relevant evidence
Assume the old conclusion is permanent
quiz.because: A changed operating condition may invalidate earlier evidence. Preserve the history so the comparison can be repeated.

given.data: A camera replacement changes input quality after the previous design review.

build.title: Review Botie’s inspection service
build.problem: Botie needs to satisfy a fault-miss requirement and a queue budget. The fault fixture and arrival trace measure different properties.
build.challenge: Count missed faults using labels and decisions. Separately replay the queue and find its maximum. Compare each quantity with its own limit, then return 1 only when both checks pass.
build.why: Separate branches preserve the meaning of each requirement. The final AND passes only after both measured quantities meet their limits.
build.limitation: This verifies two toy requirements. Field usefulness, inspection capacity, label coverage, memory, response deadlines, and fallback behaviour still need their own evidence.
hints: The fault fixture and load trace are separate branches. Start by deciding which inputs belong to each requirement.
Count labels times one minus decisions for missed faults. Separately feed arrivals and capacities through Queue over time and Largest value.
